The numbers are in num-06.out. This is what chapter 10 promises when it says that the factorization is made once and only applied at every step.

This saving has a limit that we see on the same example. With a single right-hand side the factorization saves nothing, the ratio is \(1{,}00\). The matrix also changes when we change the time step \(\Delta t\), because it contains it, and then the factorization must be computed again. In a nonlinear computation the matrix changes at every correction, as we shall see in later sections of this chapter, so there the factorization is not free. Lemma 17.28 therefore holds for the same matrix and many right-hand sides, not for many matrices.

Band storage is not the only one. COOK (PDF pp. 57-58, read) stores, for a symmetric matrix, in one array all entries from the topmost nonzero entry of each column down to the diagonal (the skyline, obris) and all the zeros between them, because a direct solver turns the zeros under the skyline into nonzero entries (fill, zapolnitev). The number of stored entries is the profile of the matrix. For the same mesh one numbering gives a profile of \(21\), another \(39\), and programs renumber by themselves. The frontal method (čelni postopek) alternates assembly and solution, so that only the part of the matrix still needed by the front that travels across the structure is in memory at one time. Iterative solvers produce no fill, but converge more slowly as the condition number grows, and use preconditioning (predpogojevanje). The book does not treat these methods and names them only because a program offers a choice between them. For the bar we compute the condition number now.

17.6.2 How many digits we lose for the bar

The condition number \(\kappa(\mat K) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) (definition 6.31) tells by how much a relative error of the right-hand side can grow in the solution, and chapter 6 estimated this as \(|\delta\vek x|/|\vek x| \le \kappa\,|\delta\vek b|/|\vek b|\). For hat functions on a bar with \(n = 4\), \(8\) and \(16\) equal elements it gave \(\kappa = 29\), \(113\) and \(438\) (matrix (6.15)), about \(1{,}7\,n^2\). Why a square, and does it still hold at \(n = 1000\)?

Take the same bar: constant cross-section \(EA\), length \(L\), clamped at \(x = 0\), free at \(x = L\), divided into \(n\) equal elements of length \(h = L/n\). The unknowns are the nodal displacements \(d_1, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the stiffness matrix is \(\mat K = (EA/h)\,\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) with the matrix

\[\mat T_{\mathrm{n}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & & & \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ & & & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{17.21}\]

in which the empty places are zeros. The number \(EA/h\) only multiplies all eigenvalues, so \(\kappa(\mat K) = \kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}})\). Let us look at the condition number of \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) in figure 17.19, on logarithmic scales, and next to it the shapes that the matrix at \(n = 10\) moves most and least.

First the axes: horizontally the number of elements \(n\), vertically the condition number \(\kappa\), both on logarithmic scales, because we care how many times it grows and not by how much. On the dashed straight line lies \((4n/\pi)^2\) and its slope is \(2\), which means that \(\kappa\) grows a hundredfold for ten times more elements. The points are the exact values of the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) and lie on the line. Why slope \(2\)? On the right the left edge is the wall in which the bar is clamped. Above is the softest shape of the matrix \(\mat T_{10}\), a smooth curve: the differences \(v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) between neighbouring displacements are small, so the ratio \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} (v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1})^2/\sum_{\mathrm{k}} v_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) of element stretches to displacements is small, and this ratio is the eigenvalue (since \(\vek v^\T\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} (v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}-1})^2\) with \(v_0 = 0\)). Below is the stiffest shape, in which neighbouring nodes move oppositely and the stretch of every element is the largest possible for the given displacements. The smallest eigenvalue falls with \(n\), the largest stays below \(4\), and their ratio is the condition number. Let us look at it exactly.

Lemma 17.29 Condition number of the bar (število občutljivosti palice)

Let \(n \ge 1\), let \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the matrix (17.21) of order \(n\) and \(\theta = \pi/\big(2(2n + 1)\big)\). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = 4\sin^2\!\big((2j - 1)\theta\big)\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\) and an eigenvector \(\vek v^{(j)}\) with entries \(v^{(j)}_{\mathrm{k}} = \sin\!\big((2j - 1)\,k\,\pi/(2n + 1)\big)\).
  2. The condition number is
    \[\kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}) = \frac{\sin^2\!\big((2n - 1)\theta\big)}{\sin^2\theta} = \frac{\cos^2\!\big(\pi/(2n + 1)\big)}{\sin^2\theta} . \tag{17.22}\]
  3. For every \(n\)
    \[\Big(\frac{2(2n + 1)}{\pi}\Big)^2 \cos^2\frac{\pi}{2n + 1} \le \kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}) \le \Big(\frac{2(2n + 1)}{\pi}\Big)^2 \frac{1}{(1 - \theta/2)^2} . \tag{17.23}\]
Proof

We must show that the listed vectors solve the eigenvalue problem, that these are all the eigenvalues, and that equation (17.22) and the estimate (17.23) follow. Write \(\varphi = (2j - 1)\pi/(2n + 1)\), so that \(v_{\mathrm{k}} = \sin k\varphi\), and also \(v_0 = 0\) and \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\).

  1. Row \(k\) of \(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}}\) for \(1 \le k \le n - 1\) gives \(-v_{\mathrm{k}-1} + 2v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) (at \(k = 1\) we have \(v_0 = 0\), which is the clamp). Row \(n\) gives \(-v_{\mathrm{n}-1} + v_{\mathrm{n}}\), which is the same form with \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\) (free end: the last element has no right neighbour).
  2. By the addition formulas (corollary 8.15) \(\sin(k - 1)\varphi + \sin(k + 1)\varphi = 2\sin k\varphi\,\cos\varphi\), so \(-v_{\mathrm{k}-1} + 2v_{\mathrm{k}} - v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = (2 - 2\cos\varphi)\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\). Since by the same theorem \(\cos\varphi = 1 - 2\sin^2(\varphi/2)\), we have \(2 - 2\cos\varphi = 4\sin^2(\varphi/2)\).
  3. The condition \(v_{\mathrm{n}+1} = v_{\mathrm{n}}\) holds, because by the addition formulas \(\sin(n + 1)\varphi - \sin n\varphi = 2\cos\!\big((n + \tfrac12)\varphi\big)\sin\tfrac{\varphi}{2}\) and \((n + \tfrac12)\varphi = (2j - 1)\pi/2\), where the cosine is zero.
  4. The vector \(\vek v^{(j)}\) is not zero, since \(v_1 = \sin\varphi \ne 0\) for \(0 < \varphi < \pi\). So \(4\sin^2(\varphi/2) = 4\sin^2\!\big((2j - 1)\theta\big)\) is an eigenvalue. The angle \((2j - 1)\theta\) lies in \((0, \pi/2)\), where \(\sin^2\) is strictly increasing, so these \(n\) values are pairwise different. A matrix of order \(n\) has at most \(n\) eigenvalues, so these are all. This is item 1.
  5. By the increase the smallest eigenvalue is at \(j = 1\) and the largest at \(j = n\), and their ratio is the first part of equation (17.22). Since \((2n - 1)\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2} - \tfrac{\pi}{2n + 1}\), we have \(\sin\!\big((2n - 1)\theta\big) = \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2n + 1}\) (addition formula), which is the second part.
  6. The estimate: by theorem 8.60 for \(\sin\) with the second derivative \(\sin\theta = \theta - \tfrac12\,\theta^2\sin\xi\) with \(0 < \xi < \theta\), so \(\theta - \theta^2/2 \le \sin\theta \le \theta\). The upper bound gives the lower bound in (17.23), since \(1/\theta^2 = (2(2n + 1)/\pi)^2\), the lower bound gives the upper one, since \(\cos^2 \le 1\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. That the condition number of an axially loaded bar grows with the square of the number of elements is stated by COOK (PDF p. 322, read, exponent \(2m/n = 2/1\)), and the lemma proves it for this bar.

The lemma says what the figure shows. The largest eigenvalue is below \(4\) and approaches it, the smallest is \(4\sin^2\theta\), about \(\pi^2/(2n + 1)^2\), so it falls as \(1/n^2\). The ratio is therefore about \((4n/\pi)^2\), and the slope \(2\) is the slope of this expression. For \(n = 4\), \(8\) and \(16\) the lemma gives \(29{,}28\), \(113{,}50\) and \(437{,}70\), exactly the \(29\), \(113\) and \(438\) of chapter 6. For larger \(n\):

\(n\) \(\kappa(\mat T_{\mathrm{n}})\) lower bound (17.23) upper bound \(\kappa/(4n/\pi)^2\) \(\log_{10}\kappa\)
\(10\) \(175{,}09\) \(174{,}76\) \(192{,}89\) \(1{,}080\) \(2{,}2\)
\(100\) \(16\,370{,}2\) \(16\,369{,}9\) \(16\,502{,}6\) \(1{,}010\) \(4{,}2\)
\(1000\) \(1\,622\,757\) \(1\,622\,756\) \(1\,624\,035\) \(1{,}001\) \(6{,}2\)

The last column is the estimate of the lost digits. COOK (PDF p. 321, read) says that with \(d\) digits in a computer number at least \(d_{\text{acc}} \ge d - \log_{10}\kappa\) digits are accurate, and that the sign \(\ge\) means that \(\log_{10}\kappa\) may overestimate the loss, which we shall see in the next section. For a bar of \(1000\) elements this is \(6{,}2\) of \(16\) digits, so at least \(16 - 6{,}2 = 9{,}8\), almost ten, remain reliable. For a bar, refining the mesh does no harm. For a beam, however, COOK (PDF p. 322) gives the exponent \(2m/n = 4/1\): \(\kappa\) grows with the fourth power of the number of elements, and doubling them increases it \(16\) times. That is \(\log_{10}16 = 1{,}2\) digits more at every doubling, for the bar only \(\log_{10}4 = 0{,}6\) digits. For a beam, refining a mesh that reduces the discretization error therefore quickly raises the numerical one.

17.6.3 When a large condition number is harmful

The condition number is an upper estimate, not a prediction. COOK (PDF p. 316, read) says that we cannot call a matrix ill-conditioned (slabo pogojena) until we state what is done with it: a matrix that is good for solving equations can be bad for eigenvalues and vice versa. The simplest example where this shows is two springs in a chain.

We set up the model. A spring of stiffness \(k_1\) is fixed to the wall, at its other end is node 1, then follows a spring of stiffness \(k_2\) and node 2, where the force \(F\) pulls. The springs are linear, massless and frictionless, and the displacements are small, so that the nodes stay on one straight line (an idealization that chapter 7 also uses). We draw the soft spring \(k_1\) as a long coil and the stiff spring \(k_2\) as a short, thick coil, because that is exactly the difference we care about. The displacement \(u_1\) is the distance between the original position of node 1 and its position after loading, the displacement \(u_2\) the same for node 2.

We write the equilibrium conditions as always, on free bodies. On node 1 the left spring pulls back with the force \(k_1 u_1\) and the right one forward with the force \(k_2(u_2 - u_1)\), because the right spring is stretched by \(u_2 - u_1\). With no external force \(k_1 u_1 = k_2(u_2 - u_1)\). On node 2 the force \(F\) pulls forward and the right spring back with the force \(k_2(u_2 - u_1)\), so \(k_2(u_2 - u_1) = F\). In matrix form

\[\begin{bmatrix} k_1 + k_2 & -k_2 \\ -k_2 & k_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ u_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ F \end{bmatrix} . \tag{17.24}\]

The solution is \(u_1 = F/k_1\) and \(u_2 = F/k_1 + F/k_2\), which we check by substituting into both equations. Let \(k_1 = 1\) and \(F = 1\) (displacements in the unit \(F/k_1\)), \(s = k_2/k_1\) the stiffness ratio, so the true displacement is \(u_2 = 1 + 1/s\). In elimination without row exchange the pivot is \(k_1 + k_2\) and the second row after the first step has the coefficient \(k_2 - k_2^2/(k_1 + k_2) = k_1 k_2/(k_1 + k_2)\). The information about \(k_1\) is hidden in this difference in the last digits of the number \(k_2\): at \(s = 10^{15}\) and \(16\) digits only one of them remains.

Lemma 17.30 Stiff spring on a soft one (toga vzmet na mehki)

Let \(k_1, k_2 > 0\), \(s = k_2/k_1\) and let \(\mat K\) be the matrix of equation (17.24). Then:

  1. The condition number \(\kappa\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is the larger solution of the equation \(\kappa + 1/\kappa = 4s + 2 + 1/s\) and
    \[4s + 1 + \frac1s < \kappa < 4s + 2 + \frac1s . \tag{17.25}\]
  2. For the unknowns \(u_1\) and \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = u_2 - u_1\) the matrix of the system is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}} = \mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) and the right-hand side \((F, F)^\T\), so \(\kappa(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}) = s\) and the solution is \(u_1 = F/k_1\), \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = F/k_2\), each with one division.
Proof

We must show the equation for \(\kappa\) and the form of the second matrix. The first item needs the trace and the determinant, the second the energy.

  1. The eigenvalues are the roots of the equation \(\lambda^2 - (k_1 + 2k_2)\lambda + k_1 k_2 = 0\), since the trace of \(\mat K\) is \(k_1 + 2k_2\) and the determinant is \((k_1 + k_2)k_2 - k_2^2 = k_1 k_2\). The discriminant \((k_1 + 2k_2)^2 - 4k_1 k_2 = k_1^2 + 4k_2^2\) is positive, so the roots are real and distinct. Their sum \(k_1 + 2k_2\) and product \(k_1 k_2\) are positive, so both are positive. We call the larger \(\lambda_{\max}\) and the smaller \(\lambda_{\min}\).
  2. From \((\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min})^2/(\lambda_{\max}\lambda_{\min}) = \kappa + 2 + 1/\kappa\) and step 1 we get \(\kappa + 2 + 1/\kappa = (k_1 + 2k_2)^2/(k_1 k_2) = 4s + 4 + 1/s\). Hence \(\kappa + 1/\kappa = 4s + 2 + 1/s\).
  3. Since the eigenvalues are distinct, \(\kappa > 1\) and \(0 < 1/\kappa < 1\). From step 2 it follows that \(\kappa < 4s + 2 + 1/s\) and \(\kappa > 4s + 1 + 1/s\).
  4. The second item. The potential energy is \(\Pi = \tfrac12 k_1 u_1^2 + \tfrac12 k_2 u_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - F u_2\) and \(u_2 = u_1 + u_{\mathrm{r}}\). By stationarity (corollary 8.58) the equations are \(\partial\Pi/\partial u_1 = k_1 u_1 - F = 0\) and \(\partial\Pi/\partial u_{\mathrm{r}} = k_2 u_{\mathrm{r}} - F = 0\), which is a diagonal system with the matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) and the right-hand side \((F, F)^\T\). The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, the ratio is \(k_2/k_1 = s\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF pp. 316-317, read) uses the same two-spring chain to explain ill-conditioning, there with \(k_1 \gg k_2\) and different notation. The relative degrees of freedom (PDF pp. 319-320) are the same idea as item 2.

The numbers for \(k_1 = 1\) (num-06.out, in agreement with c17.out):

\(s\) \(\kappa\) (lemma) error of \(u_2\) with \((u_1, u_2)\) \(4s \cdot 10^{-16}\) error of \(u_2\) with \((u_1, u_{\mathrm{r}})\)
\(10^3\) \(4{,}002 \cdot 10^3\) \(5{,}8 \cdot 10^{-14}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-13}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^6\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^6\) \(8{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-10}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^9\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^9\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-7}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^{12}\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{12}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-4}\) below \(10^{-16}\)
\(10^{15}\) \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{15}\) \(1{,}4 \cdot 10^{-1}\) \(4 \cdot 10^{-1}\) below \(10^{-16}\)

The same numbers are on the right of figure 17.20. On the axes are the stiffness ratio \(s\) horizontally and the relative error \(\varepsilon\) of the displacement \(u_2\) vertically, both on logarithmic scales, because both change by many orders of magnitude. The column \(\kappa\) says that \(\kappa \approx 4k_2/k_1\). At \(s = 10^{15}\) NumPy gives \(4{,}571 \cdot 10^{15}\) from the computed eigenvalues instead of the \(4{,}000 \cdot 10^{15}\) of the lemma (num-06.out). The smallest eigenvalue there is about \(0{,}5\), while the entries of the matrix are about \(10^{15}\), so rounding spoils it already in the computation of the eigenvalues. The column with the error for the unknowns \((u_1, u_2)\) is the displacement error measured on the computer (with the NumPy library), in the figure the orange line. It stays below the estimate \(4s \cdot 10^{-16} \approx \kappa \cdot 10^{-16}\) of the column after it, in the figure the dashed straight line, and follows it: from \(s = 10^3\) to \(s = 10^{15}\) both grow by about \(12\) orders of magnitude. At \(s = 10^{15}\) the error is \(14\) % and the result is useless, while the same system in other unknowns stays accurate. The last column, in the figure the empty blue circles, is a case where a large condition number does not mean a loss: the matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(1, s)\) has \(\kappa = s\), a quarter of the number of the matrix \(\mat K\), but loses no digit, because it contains no subtraction of nearly equal numbers. The condition number is therefore an upper estimate of the loss, not a prediction.

Two more cases show what a large condition number says and what it does not.

  • Multiply the whole matrix by \(1000\), for example by changing from N/mm to N/m. All eigenvalues are multiplied by \(1000\) and the ratio is the same: for \(\mat T_{10}\) we have \(\kappa = 175{,}0866\) before and after. A change of units in all equations at once therefore causes no bad conditioning and cures none. It is different with a change of unknowns, such as from \((u_1, u_2)\) to \((u_1, u_{\mathrm{r}})\). COOK (PDF p. 320, read) therefore proposes to compute \(\kappa\) from the matrix multiplied by a diagonal matrix so that it has ones on the diagonal, because it is then large only when the matrix is really nearly singular. For \(\mat K\) of equation (17.24) this is the matrix \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -r \\ -r & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) with \(r = \sqrt{s/(1 + s)}\), eigenvalues \(1 \pm r\) and ratio \((1 + r)/(1 - r) \approx 4s\), as large as before. For \(\mathrm{diag}(1, s)\) the same procedure gives the unit matrix and \(\kappa = 1\).
  • Load the springs differently: the force \(F\) pulls node 1 back and node 2 forward, so \(\vek f = (-F, F)^\T\), two equal and opposite forces at the ends of the stiff spring, in equilibrium together. At \(s = 10^{12}\) and \(10^{15}\) the computed stretch \(u_2 - u_1\) equals \(10^{-12}\) and \(10^{-15}\) (num-06.out), although the matrix is the same and \(\kappa\) equally large. COOK (PDF p. 317) says that under an equilibrium load the relative displacement is computed accurately even if the rigid displacement carries an error. The error is in the displacement of the whole stiff mass, not in the stretch of the spring.

When, then, do we expect trouble? When a stiff mass sits on a soft support and we care about a displacement or a force that the soft support determines (COOK, PDF p. 317, read): the information about the soft support is in the last digits of the stiff terms. A similar phenomenon is in chapter 12, where the penalty stiffness of a constraint makes \(\kappa\) grow at least as the penalty number (lemma 12.29), and in shear locking, where the stiffness of the element itself does this. Lemma 12.29 is not used here, because the matrix without the stiff spring would have to be positive definite, and the soft spring at the wall does not hold \(u_2\) at all. The kinship is therefore in the mechanism and not in the theorem. The remedy is the same as there. COOK (PDF pp. 319-320, read) names it: we choose the unknowns so that the large number does not appear off the diagonal, as \(u_1\) and \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) above, or with local axes at an inclined support.

17.6.4 What we showed

This section treated only the numerical error, the third of the three, and it does not reduce the modelling or the discretization error. The factorization is computed once and every further right-hand side costs \(2nb + n\) instead of \(n b^2/2\) (lemma 17.28), but only for the same matrix. The condition number of the bar grows as \((4n/\pi)^2\) (lemma 17.29), for a beam by COOK as \(n^4\), so a refinement that reduces the discretization error raises the numerical one. A large condition number is an upper estimate of the loss of digits: a stiff spring on a soft one has it and also suffers the loss (lemma 17.30, \(\kappa \approx 4k_2/k_1\)), the same system in relative unknowns has the number \(s\), a quarter of it, and no loss. For every result we therefore ask three questions: how much modelling error, how much discretization error and how many digits we have lost.

17.7 Nonlinear statics and imperfections

So far the model has always been linear: displacements are proportional to the load, the stiffness matrix is constant and one system of equations gives the answer. Section 17.1 set the modelling error beside the discretization error and the numerical error (definition 17.2). Here we meet the case where the linear model itself is wrong. The section treats the modelling error and the numerical error that a stopped iteration causes in a nonlinear model. It does not treat the discretization error, because we take models with one unknown and so there is no mesh. Reducing one error does not reduce the others: a Newton iteration that runs to the eighth decimal place does not repair a model that is wrong. The section answers three questions. What is different in a nonlinear model compared with a linear one? How do we solve an equation that cannot be solved directly, and what does the solution we find tell us and not tell us? Why does linear buckling analysis (definition 12.51) predict, for some columns, a load that is never reached?

17.7.1 Two models of a column

We take the simplest column that shows buckling. A rigid bar of length \(L\) is attached at the bottom by a pin, a support that lets the bar only rotate. The bar is rigid, so it does not bend and its position is a single angle \(\theta\) measured from the vertical (angle \(\theta\)). At its top a vertical force \(P\) acts downwards. The force is a load (obremenitev), a force that we apply to the body from outside. It stays vertical even when the bar tilts. A spring holds the bar upright, and we compare two ways of doing it. In model (i) a rotational spring of stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{r}}\) (moment per radian) sits in the pin, as in example 8.66. In model (ii) a horizontal spring of stiffness \(k\) (force per length) joins the top of the bar to a wall. Both springs are linear, only the geometry brings nonlinearity: the angle \(\theta\) enters the equations through \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\). We call such a source geometric nonlinearity (geometrijska nelinearnost), because we write equilibrium on the tilted position, not on the initial one.

A real bar is not perfectly straight, the load is not exactly on the axis and the support is not perfect. We capture these departures with one number: the springs are unstretched at the angle \(\theta_0\), not at \(\theta = 0\), which the dashed position \(\theta_0\) shows in the figure. We call \(\theta_0\) the imperfection (nepopolnost), since a perfect column (\(\theta_0 = 0\)) cannot be reached in any workshop. With \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad the top of a bar of length \(L = 1\) m is displaced from the vertical by \(L\sin\theta_0 = 10{,}00\) mm. This is the size of imperfection we shall compute. The idealizations are written in brackets: the bar is rigid, the springs are linear and, in model (ii), horizontal, the force stays vertical.

We write the energy of model (ii) as in example 8.66. The spring is stretched by \(L(\sin\theta - \sin\theta_0)\), because the horizontal distance of the top from the vertical through the pin is \(L\sin\theta\) and the spring is unstretched at \(L\sin\theta_0\). The height of the top is \(L\cos\theta\), so the energy of the load is \(P L\cos\theta\). With \(s_0 = \sin\theta_0\),

\[V(\theta) = \tfrac12\,k L^2\,(\sin\theta - s_0)^2 + P L\cos\theta . \tag{17.26}\]

Model (i) has \(V = \tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{r}}(\theta - \theta_0)^2 + P L\cos\theta\). By corollary 8.58 equilibrium is a stationary point of the energy, \(V'(\theta) = 0\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81) the derivative is \(V' = kL^2(\sin\theta - s_0)\cos\theta - P L\sin\theta\). We write the load as the share \(p = P/(kL)\) of the number \(kL\), which we shall meet at once as the critical load, and divide the derivative by \(kL^2\):

\[g(\theta; p) = \frac{V'(\theta)}{kL^2} = (\sin\theta - s_0)\cos\theta - p\,\sin\theta . \tag{17.27}\]

The number \(g\) tells how much generalized force (with the opposite sign, \(g = -Q/(kL^2)\) by definition 8.53) remains unbalanced on the bar, so we call it the imbalance (neuravnoteženost). Equilibrium is \(g = 0\).

Let us test what nonlinearity changes, on model (ii) with \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad (NumPy). At \(p = 0{,}45\) the bar rotates from \(\theta_0\) by \(0{,}008185\) rad, at the doubled \(p = 0{,}9\) by \(0{,}095491\) rad, that is \(11{,}7\) times more, not twice. There is no superposition. At \(p = 0{,}9\) the equation \(g = 0\) has three solutions in \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\), namely \(\theta = -0{,}4921\), \(0{,}1055\) and \(0{,}3919\) rad. The equilibrium paths are in the lower part of the figure: on the axes the horizontal is the angle \(\theta\) and the vertical \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). The last two are, on the orange path, the intersections of the horizontal line \(p = 0{,}9\) with the middle curve for \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\), the first is at a negative angle outside the figure. Which is the real position of the bar? The answer is in theorem 8.63. The second derivatives \(V''/(kL^2)\) are \(-0{,}2444\), \(+0{,}0839\) and \(-0{,}1197\), so only the middle one is stable (definition 8.64). These are three of the properties that COOK (PDF p. 610) lists for nonlinear equations: superposition does not hold, each load case needs its own analysis and for a given load there can be more than one solution. The fourth, that reversing the order of loading can change the result, stays with COOK.

COOK (PDF pp. 609 and 610) distinguishes three kinds of nonlinearity: material, where material properties are functions of stress or strain (plasticity, creep), contact, where a gap opens or closes, and geometric. In all three the stiffness matrix, sometimes the right-hand side too, becomes a function of the displacements: \(\mat K(\vek D)\,\vek D = \vek R\). We cannot compute the displacements directly, because \(\mat K\) needs the displacements. This section treats only geometric nonlinearity on models with one unknown. Material and contact nonlinearity are named, not treated (for contact see chapter 25, plasticity is not in the book). A limit of models with one unknown is that they do not show how Newton's method deals with a matrix of size one thousand.

17.7.2 Tangent stiffness and Newton's method

For a nonlinear equation \(g(\theta) = 0\) we cannot find the root in one step, but we can solve a linear equation. The idea is the same as for the derivative: at a point we know, we replace the curve by its tangent and find the zero of the tangent. So we first name the slope.

Definition 17.31 Tangent stiffness (tangentna togost)

Let a system have \(n\) generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) in an open set \(D \subset \mathbb R^n\) and a twice continuously differentiable potential energy \(V\) (definition 8.53). The imbalance column \(\vek g(\vek q)\) of \(n\) numbers has components \(g_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\), so \(\vek g = -\vek Q\). By corollary 8.58 the point \(\vek q\) is an equilibrium exactly when \(\vek g(\vek q) = \vek 0\). The tangent stiffness at \(\vek q\) is the \(n \times n\) matrix

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q) = \frac{\partial\vek g}{\partial\vek q}(\vek q) , \qquad (\mat K_{\mathrm{t}})_{\mathrm{sr}} = \frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}\,\partial q_{\mathrm{r}}} , \tag{17.28}\]

the Hessian matrix of the energy (definition 8.61). For one coordinate it is the number \(V''(q)\). If \(\vek q^\ast\) is an equilibrium, positive definiteness of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q^\ast)\) tells by theorem 8.63 that the equilibrium is energetically stable.

Source: COOK (PDF p. 610) for one unknown: \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}u\), the slope of the graph of force against displacement. The definition with the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is ours.

The name is so because \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the slope of the tangent to the graph of the imbalance. For a linear structure with the energy \(\tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q - \vek R^\T\vek q\) we have \(\vek g = \mat K\vek q - \vek R\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}} = \mat K\), the constant stiffness matrix of chapters 7 and 12. For a nonlinear one \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is different at every position. For our model (ii), differentiating the right-hand side of (17.27) by the product rule,

\[\frac{K_{\mathrm{t}}}{kL^2} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta} = \cos^2\theta - (\sin\theta - s_0)\sin\theta - p\cos\theta . \tag{17.29}\]

At the straight perfect position (\(\theta = 0\), \(s_0 = 0\)) we have \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = 1 - p\). The one is the elastic part of the spring and the term \(-p\) is the part that the compressive load takes away, as in equation (12.56), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} + \mu\,\mat G_{\mathrm{ff}}\). The zero is at \(p = 1\), so the critical load of the perfect model (ii) is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = kL\). For model (i) it is \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = k_{\mathrm{r}}/L\) by example 8.66.

Definition 17.32 Newton's method (Newtonova metoda)

Let \(\vek g\colon D \to \mathbb R^n\) be the imbalance of definition 17.31 at a given load and \(\vek q^{(0)} \in D\) a starting estimate. Step \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) is: solve the linear system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q^{(k)})\,\Delta\vek q = -\vek g(\vek q^{(k)})\) and put \(\vek q^{(k+1)} = \vek q^{(k)} + \Delta\vek q\). We stop when the imbalance is small enough (the measure is in the text below). For one unknown, \(\theta^{(k+1)} = \theta^{(k)} - g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)})\).

Source: COOK (PDF p. 611) says that the method is called Newton's method in calculus texts and Newton-Raphson (N-R) in structural mechanics, and describes it as a way of generating the curve of load against displacement. The notation is ours.

The name is Newton's, as COOK (PDF p. 611) says, why the name Raphson is added in structural mechanics the source does not say. Figure 17.22 shows the method on model (ii) at \(p = 0{,}9\). On the left panel the horizontal is the angle \(\theta\), the vertical the imbalance \(g\) (heights are enlarged 250 times in the figure). The blue curve is the graph of \(g(\theta; 0{,}9)\). We start at the point \(\theta^{(0)} = \theta_0 = 0{,}01\), where \(g = -0{,}009\). Through this point we draw the tangent with the slope \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and find where it crosses the axis: that is \(\theta^{(1)} = 0{,}100048\). The next tangent is already so near the curve that we cannot tell them apart in the figure. The remaining iterates are \(0{,}1054390\) and \(0{,}1054914\), and the root is \(\theta^\ast = 0{,}10549145\).

Does this procedure always converge, and how fast? A theorem answers for one unknown. In it we use Taylor's theorem with the second derivative (theorem 8.60), the only tool of this kind in this section.

Theorem 17.33 Quadratic convergence of Newton's method (kvadratična konvergenca Newtonove metode)

Let \(g\) be a twice continuously differentiable function of one variable on the closed interval \(I = [\theta^\ast - r, \theta^\ast + r]\) with \(g(\theta^\ast) = 0\). Let \(m > 0\) and \(M\) be numbers with \(|g'(\theta)| \ge m\) and \(|g''(\theta)| \le M\) for every \(\theta \in I\). Let \(K = M/(2m)\). If the starting estimate \(\theta^{(0)} \in I\) and \(K\,|\theta^{(0)} - \theta^\ast| < 1\), all iterates \(\theta^{(k)}\) of Newton's method lie in \(I\) and the error \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = \theta^{(k)} - \theta^\ast\) satisfies

\[|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 , \qquad K\,|e_{\mathrm{k}}| \le \big(K\,|e_0|\big)^{2^k} . \tag{17.30}\]
Proof

We must show the one-step error estimate and then, by induction, that the iterates stay in \(I\) and the error falls.

  1. Let \(\theta^{(k)} \in I\) and \(e_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\). By theorem 8.60 with \(x_0 = \theta^{(k)}\) and \(x = \theta^\ast\) there is a point \(c\) between them, hence in \(I\), with \(0 = g(\theta^\ast) = g(\theta^{(k)}) - g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12 g''(c)\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\).
  2. Since \(|g'(\theta^{(k)})| \ge m > 0\) we may divide by \(g'(\theta^{(k)})\): \(0 = g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)}) - e_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\,g''(c)/g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). By definition 17.32, \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = e_{\mathrm{k}} - g(\theta^{(k)})/g'(\theta^{(k)})\). So \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \tfrac12\,g''(c)/g'(\theta^{(k)})\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\).
  3. From \(|g''| \le M\) and \(|g'| \ge m\) it follows that \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). If \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\), then \(\theta^{(k)}\) is a root and the estimate holds.
  4. Let \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} = K|e_{\mathrm{k}}|\). Step 3 gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le \delta_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). Since \(\delta_0 < 1\), induction gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} \le \delta_0^{2^k}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} < 1\) for every \(k\).
  5. From \(\delta_{\mathrm{k}} < 1\) it follows that \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}| \le K\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = \delta_{\mathrm{k}}\,|e_{\mathrm{k}}| < |e_{\mathrm{k}}| \le r\), so \(\theta^{(k+1)} \in I\) and step 1 holds for every \(k\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF p. 612) says that the errors of Newton's method usually fall, and adds that convergence is not guaranteed for every nonlinear problem.

The theorem says that the number of correct decimals roughly doubles after each step. We check it on figure 17.22, left. The errors at \(p = 0{,}9\) are \(e_0 = 9{,}55\cdot 10^{-2}\), \(5{,}44\cdot 10^{-3}\), \(5{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(5{,}16\cdot 10^{-9}\) and the ratios \(|e_{\mathrm{k}+1}|/e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) are \(0{,}60\), \(1{,}77\) and \(1{,}87\). By step 2 the ratio must tend to \(|g''(\theta^\ast)|/(2\,g'(\theta^\ast)) = 0{,}3141/(2\cdot 0{,}08388) = 1{,}87\) (the numbers \(g''\) and \(g'\) are from NumPy at the root), and it does. We did not compute the constants \(m\) and \(M\) for the whole interval \(I\). The theorem guarantees convergence, here we observe it in the ratios.

Example 17.34 Where the theorem fails: zero stiffness and the wrong root (kje izrek ne velja: ničelna togost in napačen koren)

Theorem 17.33 has two hypotheses that a column can lose: \(|g'| \ge m > 0\) on the interval \(I\) and a starting estimate close to the root (\(K\,|e_0| < 1\)). For each we show a case where it is missing.

The first is \(m = 0\), that is \(g'(\theta^\ast) = 0\). For \(g(x) = x^2\) the root is \(0\) and \(g' = 2x\), so \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{k}}^2/(2x_{\mathrm{k}}) = x_{\mathrm{k}}/2\), the iterates are \(1\), \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}25\), \(0{,}125\). The error only halves at each step, the convergence is linear. In our model the stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at the limit load: the curve of the left panel would, at \(p = 0{,}93119\), only touch the axis and the tangent at the root would be horizontal. As we approach the limit load \(0{,}93119\) at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\), Newton's method needs more and more iterations: at \(p = 0{,}9\), \(0{,}92\), \(0{,}93\) and \(0{,}931\) these are \(4\), \(5\), \(6\) and \(7\) iterations for an imbalance below \(10^{-13}\), and the stiffness at the root is \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = 0{,}0839\), \(0{,}0506\), \(0{,}0173\) and \(0{,}0071\).

The second is a start far from the root, and with it the root that the method finds. At \(p = 0{,}95\), above the limit load, the right panel of figure 17.22 shows that the graph of \(g\) does not cross the axis on the right side. From the start \(\theta^{(0)} = 0{,}01\) the iterates along the tangents are \(0{,}2002\), \(-0{,}2708\), \(-0{,}4877\), \(-0{,}4087\), \(-0{,}3895\) and after eight steps \(-0{,}388299\). The hypothesis of the theorem is missing here: \(g'(0{,}01) = 0{,}050 > 0\) while \(g' < 0\) at the root, so \(g'\) has a zero between the start and the root and there is no interval \(I\) with \(m > 0\) that holds both. At the end, when the iterates are near the root, the convergence is quadratic, as the theorem promises. But the root is an equilibrium with \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = -0{,}16976 < 0\), which by theorem 8.63 (part 2) is not energetically stable. At \(p = 0{,}95\) it is the only equilibrium in \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) (NumPy). So the convergence of Newton's method says nothing about stability, it only guarantees that the imbalance is zero. If we start from the last solution at \(p = 0{,}9\) instead of from \(\theta_0\), the first seven iterates jump between \(0{,}13\) and \(0{,}36\) rad, then the method leaps away and after \(15\) steps stops at \(\theta = -9{,}43\) rad. This is a root of the equation because of the periodicity of the sine, not a position of the bar we modelled.

Newton's method needs the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and a solution of a system at every step. For a large system this is the most expensive part (the factorization of lemma 7.47, the cost by section 17.6). The modified Newton-Raphson method (spremenjena Newtonova metoda) uses the same \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\), computed at the starting position, in all steps, so it computes the factorization once (COOK, PDF p. 612). On our example (\(p = 0{,}9\)) it needs \(15\) iterations instead of \(4\) to reach an imbalance below \(10^{-14}\) and the error falls at each step only to \(0{,}16\) of the previous one, which is linear convergence. The saving is in the cost of a step, not in the number of steps.

How do we choose the starting estimate and when do we stop? COOK (PDF p. 612) recommends applying the load in steps and starting each time from the solution of the previous one. At \(p = 0{,}3\), \(0{,}6\) and \(0{,}9\), starting from the previous solution, we get \(\theta = 0{,}014287\), \(0{,}025014\) and \(0{,}105491\) rad with \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\) iterations, and one step to \(p = 0{,}9\) needs \(4\) too. For such mild nonlinearity there is no saving, not even just below the limit load: at \(p = 0{,}931\) one step from \(\theta_0\) finds the stable position \(0{,}20592\) rad in \(7\) iterations, and a step from the solution at \(p = 0{,}93\) finds the same position in \(5\). The steps pay off in another way. Each gives one point of the path, as COOK (PDF p. 611) describes the method, and when the load exceeds the limit load, the iteration from the last solution no longer finds a nearby equilibrium and jumps far away, as in example 17.34. We stop when the imbalance is a small share of the load and the step a small share of the initial step (COOK, PDF pp. 615 and 616, tolerances between \(0{,}001\) and \(0{,}01\)). We denote the tolerance by \(\delta\). Here the measure is \(|g| \le \delta\,p\), since \(P L = p\,kL^2\) is the moment that the load contributes. With \(\delta = 10^{-3}\) and \(p = 0{,}9\) the method stops already after the first step: \(|g| = 4{,}6\cdot 10^{-4} < 9\cdot 10^{-4}\). But \(\theta^{(1)}\) has an error of \(5{,}4\cdot 10^{-3}\) rad, which is \(5{,}2\) % of \(\theta^\ast\), since the error is about \(g/K_{\mathrm{t}} = 4{,}6\cdot 10^{-4}/0{,}0839\). A small imbalance with a small stiffness means a large displacement error. COOK (PDF p. 616) warns that the displacement criterion alone is not sufficient and should be supplemented by the force criterion. Our example shows the opposite side: the force criterion alone is too lenient at small stiffness. So we use both. When we reach \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) we have a limit point and the method fails, as example 17.34 shows. COOK (PDF p. 613) describes the arc-length method (metoda dolžine loka), which changes the load during the iterations so that the points lie on a circle around the starting point, and can pass a limit point. We only name it, we do not compute it.

17.7.3 Imperfections and the limit load

What do the two models say about a column? The load that linear buckling analysis predicts for a column is, by definition 12.51, the first \(\mu\) at which \(\mat K + \mu\,\mat G\) is singular. For both models this is the same: the stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) at \(\theta = 0\) is zero at \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), for (i) at \(k_{\mathrm{r}}/L\), for (ii) at \(kL\). Linear analysis reads only the zero of \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) and does not tell apart two models that do not differ in it. They differ in where the bar goes when \(P\) exceeds \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), and the figure of the paths shows it.

The perfect model (i) has, by example 8.66, the bent branch \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \theta/\sin\theta \ge 1\), which rises and is stable: a column that bends still carries more load. The same holds for the continuous perfect column: by theorem 8.132 \(P/P_{\mathrm{cr}} = (2K(k)/\pi)^2\), and at the tip angle \(\alpha = 0{,}5\), \(1{,}0\) and \(\pi/2\) rad this is \(1{,}032\), \(1{,}137\) and \(1{,}393\) (NumPy, \(K\) by the arithmetic-geometric mean). In the perfect model (ii) the opposite happens. At \(s_0 = 0\) we have \(g = \sin\theta\,(\cos\theta - p)\), so equilibrium \(\theta = 0\) and the branch \(p = \cos\theta\), which falls. By equation (17.29) on this branch \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta - \cos^2\theta = -\sin^2\theta < 0\), so it is not stable by theorem 8.63 (part 2). The energy at the critical point shows it too. At \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the energy of the perfect model (i) is \(V - V(0) = k_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\theta^2/2 - 1 + \cos\theta) > 0\) for \(\theta \ne 0\) (equation (8.57)), and for (ii), with \(\sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta\),

\[V(\theta) - V(0) = kL^2\big(\tfrac12\sin^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1\big) = -\tfrac12\,kL^2\,(1 - \cos\theta)^2 < 0 . \tag{17.31}\]

The straight position of model (ii) at the critical load is not energetically stable (definition 8.64), since every other position has lower energy. At \(\theta = 0{,}1\) and \(0{,}5\) rad the difference is \(-1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\,kL^2\) and \(-7{,}49\cdot 10^{-3}\,kL^2\), and for (i) it is \(+4{,}2\cdot 10^{-6}\,k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(+2{,}6\cdot 10^{-3}\,k_{\mathrm{r}}\). The same \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), the opposite decision: this is why linear buckling analysis must stay a first step, not a verdict.

A perfect column cannot be reached, so the imperfect one interests us. For model (i) the outcome of example 8.66 is mild: all equilibria on the path from the unloaded position \(\theta_0\) are stable, the path rises smoothly, there is no limit load (thin blue curve). For model (ii) an equilibrium with \(\theta > \theta_0\) at load \(p\) is a solution of \(p = f(\theta)\), where

\[f(\theta) = \Big(1 - \frac{s_0}{\sin\theta}\Big)\cos\theta . \tag{17.32}\]

This expression is the same as \(g = 0\), since \(g = \sin\theta\,\big(f(\theta) - p\big)\). The orange curves in the figure are \(p = f(\theta)\) for three imperfections. The function \(f\) is zero at \(\theta_0\) and \(\pi/2\) and positive between, so it has a largest value on \([\theta_0, \pi/2]\) (the maximum theorem, 8.26 for one variable). We call this value the limit load (mejna sila), because it is the bound of the load above which there is no equilibrium with \(\theta\) near \(\theta_0\) (example 8.67, limit point). The word bound matters here: from this load on, a bar loaded gradually cannot stay near its previous position and moves far away, as in the snap-through (preskok) of example 8.67.

Theorem 17.35 Limit load of the imperfect column (mejna sila nepopolnega stebra)

Let model (ii) have the imperfection \(\theta_0 \in (0, \pi/2)\), \(s_0 = \sin\theta_0\), and let \(f\) be the function of equation (17.32) on \([\theta_0, \pi/2]\). Let \(p_\mathrm{lim}\) be its largest value, the limit load \(P_\mathrm{lim} = p_\mathrm{lim}\,P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). Then:

  1. At an equilibrium \(p = f(\theta)\) with \(\theta \in (\theta_0, \pi/2)\) we have \(V''(\theta) = kL^2\sin\theta\,f'(\theta)\). The equilibrium is energetically stable if \(f'(\theta) > 0\) and is not if \(f'(\theta) < 0\).
  2. For \(p > p_\mathrm{lim}\) there is no equilibrium in \((\theta_0, \pi/2)\).
  3. \(1 - \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3} \le p_\mathrm{lim} \le 1 - \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3} + \tfrac12\,s_0\).
Proof

We must show the second derivative at equilibrium, then an upper and a lower bound of the largest value by two estimates of \(\cos\theta\).

  1. For \(\theta \in (\theta_0, \pi/2)\) we have \(\sin\theta > 0\) and \(V'(\theta) = kL^2\sin\theta\,\big(f(\theta) - p\big)\). By the product rule \(V'' = kL^2\cos\theta\,(f - p) + kL^2\sin\theta\,f'\), the first term is zero at equilibrium. The rest follows from theorem 8.63 (part 1 for \(f' > 0\), part 2 for \(f' < 0\), since \(\sin\theta > 0\)).
  2. Since \(p_\mathrm{lim}\) is the largest value of \(f\), for \(p > p_\mathrm{lim}\) the equation \(f(\theta) = p\) has no solution.
  3. For \(x \in [0, 1]\) we have \(\sqrt{1 - x} \le 1 - x/2\), because after squaring \(1 - x \le 1 - x + x^2/4\). Also \(\sqrt{1 - x} \ge (1 - x)(1 + x/2) = 1 - x/2 - x^2/2\), which for \(x = 1\) holds as \(0 = 0\), and for \(x < 1\), after dividing by \(\sqrt{1 - x} > 0\), is \(1 \ge \sqrt{1 - x}\,(1 + x/2)\), after squaring \(1 \ge (1 - x)(1 + x + x^2/4) = 1 - \tfrac34 x^2 - \tfrac14 x^3\), which holds. With \(x = s^2\), \(s = \sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\) for \(\theta \in [0, \pi/2]\) we get \(1 - s^2/2 - s^4/2 \le \cos\theta \le 1 - s^2/2\).
  4. Upper bound. Since \(1 - s_0/s \ge 0\) for \(s \ge s_0\), by step 3 \(f \le (1 - s_0/s)(1 - s^2/2) = 1 - s_0/s - s^2/2 + s_0 s/2 \le 1 - (s_0/s + s^2/2) + s_0/2\), because \(s \le 1\).
  5. The inequality of the arithmetic and geometric means for three positive numbers, \(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 \ge 3\,(a_1 a_2 a_3)^{1/3}\), with \(a_1 = a_2 = s_0/(2s)\) and \(a_3 = s^2/2\), gives \(s_0/s + s^2/2 \ge 3\,(s_0^2/8)^{1/3} = \tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3}\). Hence \(f \le 1 - \tfrac32 s_0^{2/3} + \tfrac12 s_0\) and so is \(p_\mathrm{lim}\).
  6. Lower bound. Let \(s_1 = s_0^{1/3}\) and \(a = s_0^{2/3} = s_1^2\). Since \(s_0 < 1\), we have \(s_0 < s_1 < 1\), so \(\theta_1 = \arcsin s_1\) lies in \((\theta_0, \pi/2)\). By step 3, \(\cos\theta_1 \ge 1 - a/2 - a^2/2\) and \(1 - s_0/s_1 = 1 - a \ge 0\), so \(f(\theta_1) \ge (1 - a)(1 - a/2 - a^2/2) = 1 - \tfrac32 a + \tfrac12 a^3 \ge 1 - \tfrac32 a\). Since \(p_\mathrm{lim} \ge f(\theta_1)\), the lower bound is proved.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF p. 668) calls a structure whose limit load is strongly affected by small changes of geometry, load or support imperfection-sensitive and gives no formula for the law. The name of the author of this phenomenon is not on that page, so we name it after no one.

The theorem says that the loss \(1 - p_\mathrm{lim}\) equals \(\tfrac32\,s_0^{2/3}\) to within \(\tfrac12 s_0\), it is not proportional to \(s_0\): for small \(s_0\), \(s_0^{2/3}\) is much larger than \(s_0\) (at \(s_0 = 0{,}01\), \(s_0^{2/3} = 0{,}046\)). Numbers from NumPy, which checks the theorem (largest value over a grid of \(2\cdot 10^6\) points):

\(\theta_0\) (rad) 0,001 0,01 0,05
\(p_\mathrm{lim}\) 0,98504 0,93119 0,80354
at the angle \(\theta\) (rad) 0,1002 0,2171 0,3772
lower bound 0,98500 0,93038 0,79648
upper bound 0,98550 0,93538 0,82146
loss \(1 - p_\mathrm{lim}\) 1,50 % 6,88 % 19,65 %

With \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad, that is 10 mm on 1 m, the column carries only \(0{,}931\) of the critical load, with \(\theta_0 = 0{,}05\) rad, 50 mm per metre, only \(0{,}804\). A tenfold smaller imperfection gives how much smaller a loss? The law says \(10^{2/3} = 4{,}64\): a tenfold smaller imperfection (\(0{,}001\) instead of \(0{,}01\) rad) reduces the loss from \(6{,}9\) % only to \(1{,}5\) %, not to a tenth. The largest error within the bounds of the theorem (the unknown term up to \(s_0/2\)) at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\) rad is \(0{,}005\), which is \(7\) % of the loss \(6{,}9\) %. The bounds in the table lie below and above the computed value.

Do real columns lose this much? COOK (PDF p. 668) states that the limit load of real thin shells may be only about \(10\) % of the load of linear buckling analysis, and about \(50\) % in the laboratory with great effort. For a plane frame of bars with a cross section of 8 mm × 8 mm (\(E = 200\) GPa) COOK (PDF pp. 669 and 670) gives linear buckling at \(137\) N, and the perfect nonlinear analysis shows that the frame does not buckle at all. When node \(D\) is moved 2 mm sideways, linear buckling is at \(114\) N and the nonlinear analysis gives snap-through at \(86\) N, which is \(0{,}754\) of the load of linear analysis. Our model (ii) with the imperfection \(2/480 = 0{,}0042\) gives by the law \(1{,}5\,s_0^{2/3}\) a loss of \(3{,}9\) %, the frame loses \(25\) % (against the \(137\) N of the perfect frame, \(37\) %). The difference is not surprising: the frame is not one rigid bar with one spring. The model shows the mechanism and the form of the law, not the number of this frame. It also shows what COOK (PDF p. 668) says about models: the imperfection must be introduced deliberately, because small numerical errors do not steer the computation into an imperfect mode. In our perfect model (ii) with \(p = 1{,}1\) and the start at \(\theta = 0\) we have exactly \(g(0) = 0\), and Newton's method stays at \(\theta = 0\): the straight position, where \(K_{\mathrm{t}}/(kL^2) = -0{,}100 < 0\) and which is not stable. The imperfection we introduce can be the buckling mode of linear buckling analysis (COOK, PDF p. 668), so linear analysis stays a useful first step.

What does the theorem cover and what not? It is proved for model (ii). That the same law holds for every column with an unstable perfect path the section does not prove, COOK (PDF pp. 668 and 669) shows the phenomenon on shells and on a frame with numbers. For the continuous column, theorem 8.132, theorem 8.131 and theorem 12.53 are about the perfect column, an imperfect continuous column needs its own model.

17.7.4 Summary of the section

A nonlinear model has the imbalance \(\vek g(\vek q) = \vek 0\) and the tangent stiffness \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}(\vek q)\) of definition 17.31. Newton's method (definition 17.32) solves \(\vek g = \vek 0\) with tangents. By theorem 17.33 the convergence is quadratic if \(K_{\mathrm{t}} \ne 0\) at the root and the starting estimate is close enough to the root. Example 17.34 showed that at \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) it becomes linear and that convergence says nothing about the stability of the equilibrium found. Linear buckling analysis gives the same critical load for two columns that only the energy and the imperfection tell apart. In model (ii) the limit load with imperfection \(\theta_0\) is lower by about \(\tfrac32\,\sin^{2/3}\theta_0\) (theorem 17.35). The three errors: the modelling error is that the linear model knows nothing of the limit load, the numerical error is the stopped iteration (\(5{,}2\) % at a premature stop), there is no discretization error. Nonlinear dynamics follows in the next section.

17.8 Nonlinear dynamics and numerical damping

A pendulum of length \(l = 1\) m is released from the position in which the rod is horizontal. For small deflections the period would be \(2\pi\sqrt{l/g} = 2{,}006\) s, but at a deflection of \(90°\) it is \(2{,}368\) s by theorem 8.123, which is \(18\) % longer. The linear model does not suffice here, because the force on the pendulum is not a linear function of the deflection. In section 17.7 we solved such equations in statics with Newton's method. Now the question is about time: how do we step the equation of motion when the force is nonlinear, and how do we prevent the scheme of chapter 10 from exciting oscillations in the mesh that the model does not have at all?

After section 17.1 (definition 17.2) this section treats the other two kinds of error: the error of discretizing time with a step \(\Delta t\) and the numerical error of the stopped iterations of Newton's method. The modelling error is not reduced: the pendulum is a model of a rigid rod and a point mass, without friction in the pivot and without air. Reducing the step does not reduce the mesh error of section 17.3 either, because the two errors add.

17.8.1 The Newmark family (Newmarkova družina)

In chapter 10 we met two schemes. The trapezoidal rule (definition 10.63) is implicit and unconditionally stable without damping. Central differences (definition 10.68) are explicit and stable only below the critical step. We write both with the same idea: the velocity and the displacement at the end of the step are known from the start of the step and from the acceleration, and the acceleration is fixed by the equation of motion at the end of the step. They differ in how the acceleration is averaged over the step. The velocity changes over a step by \(\Delta t\) times the mean acceleration, so we replace it by the weighted sum \((1 - \gamma)\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) with two weights that add to \(1\). For the displacement we take, for each component, the expansion with a Taylor remainder (theorem 8.60): \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\Delta t^2\,a(\xi)\) with a point \(\xi\) in the step that may differ from component to component. We replace the term \(\tfrac12 a(\xi)\) by a weighted sum of \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) with the weights \(\tfrac12 - \beta\) and \(\beta\), which add to \(\tfrac12\). Two numbers, \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), are therefore free, and each pair gives its own scheme. That is why we call it a family. It is named after N. M. Newmark, who proposed it (COOK §11.13, PDF p. 432, BATHE §9.2.3, PDF p. 794). In this section the letters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) mean only these two parameters, not the shear strain of chapter 1 or anything else.

Definition 17.36 Newmark family (Newmarkova družina)

Let \(\mat M\) be a positive definite and \(\mat C\) and \(\mat K\) symmetric matrices of order \(n\), \(\vek Q(t)\) a column of forces, \(\Delta t > 0\) a step, \(\vek q_0\) and \(\vek v_0\) the initial columns, and \(\gamma\) and \(\beta \ge 0\) real numbers. The Newmark scheme with parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) is the sequence of columns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) determined by the initial columns, by equation (10.73) at \(k = 0\) (which gives \(\vek a_0\)) and, for every \(k \ge 0\), by the two equations

\[\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t^2\Big(\big(\tfrac12 - \beta\big)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \beta\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\Big) , \tag{17.33}\]
\[\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\Big((1 - \gamma)\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\Big) , \tag{17.34}\]

together with equation (10.73) at \(k + 1\). At \(\beta = 0\) the scheme is explicit (equation (17.33) does not contain \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\)), at \(\beta > 0\) it is implicit.

Source: COOK (11.13-3), PDF p. 432, with parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\). BATHE (9.18) and (9.19), PDF p. 794, with parameters \(\delta = \gamma\) and \(\alpha = \beta\). The reason with weights above is ours.

Both schemes of chapter 10 are in the family.

Lemma 17.37 The trapezoidal rule and central differences in the Newmark family (Trapezno pravilo in centralne diference v Newmarkovi družini)
  1. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) and \(\beta = \tfrac14\) the Newmark scheme is the trapezoidal rule of definition 10.63.
  2. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\) the sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) satisfies equation (10.82) at \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and coincides with the central differences of definition 10.68.
Proof

We show that equations (17.33) and (17.34) turn into the equations of chapter 10.

  1. At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) equation (17.34) is equation (10.75). At \(\beta = \tfrac14\) the right side of equation (17.33) equals \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\). From equation (10.75) we have \(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), so this is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), which is equation (10.74). This is point 1.
  2. At \(\beta = 0\) we have \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert equation (17.34) with \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) into the same expression for step \(k + 1\): \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+2} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{2}\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\).
  3. We subtract the first equality from the second: \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+2} - 2\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \Delta t^2\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). Since \(\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = -\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) at \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\), this is equation (10.82) at index \(k + 1\). The start \(\vek q_1 = \vek q_0 + \Delta t\,\vek v_0 + \tfrac12\Delta t^2\vek a_0\) is the start of definition 10.68. This is point 2.

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 432): "average acceleration" is \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\). BATHE §9.2.3 (PDF p. 794): the same as the "constant-average-acceleration method (also called trapezoidal rule)". The sources do not state point 2 in this form. The proof is not from a source.

Figure 17.23 shows the family in the plane of the parameters. We draw a horizontal axis \(\gamma\) and a vertical axis \(\beta\). Both parameters lie on them, and every point of the plane is one scheme. The first point is the trapezoidal rule at \(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\), which lemma 17.37 places in the family. Below it on the same vertical are \(\beta = \tfrac16\), the linear acceleration scheme that COOK and BATHE name (COOK PDF p. 432, BATHE PDF p. 794), and \(\beta = 0\), central differences by point 2 of the lemma. Both are only conditionally stable (COOK (11.13-8), PDF p. 433), and for central differences theorem 10.70 proves it. The blue region is the region of unconditional stability for linear equations: \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) (COOK (11.13-7), PDF p. 433, not proved here). We shall prove less, but enough for our use, namely for the line of the family \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\), which lies inside the region at \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\), because \(\beta - \gamma/2 = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4 - \gamma/2 = (\gamma - \tfrac12)^2/4 \ge 0\), so \(2\beta \ge \gamma\). On it also lie \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) with \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) with \(\beta = 0{,}36\), which we shall compare with the trapezoidal rule. The reason for this line is in the step that we compute now.

17.8.2 The step for one mode (Korak za en način)

As with the trapezoidal rule we test the scheme on one mode, since at \(\mat C = \mat 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) it splits by modes. Mode \(r\) has the eigenpair \((\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) of theorem 10.13, the coordinate \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\). The quantity \(p\) has the same unit as \(\eta\), so we can build one column \((\eta, p)\) from the two. The scheme takes a step with this column as with a matrix \(\mat A\) that has two rows and two columns. The reader knows the matrix, its trace (sled, the sum of the diagonal elements) and its determinant. An eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat A\) is a number \(\lambda\) for which the equation \(\mat A\vek x = \lambda\vek x\) has a nonzero solution. For two rows these two numbers are the roots of the equation \(\lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,\lambda + \det\mat A = 0\). The spectral radius (spektralni polmer) \(\rho(\mat A)\) is the largest absolute value among the eigenvalues. It is called a radius because all eigenvalues lie in the complex plane in the disc of this radius around the origin. Writing it with the matrix, \(\rho(\mat A)\), tells it apart from the density \(\rho\) of other chapters.

Lemma 17.38 One step of the Newmark scheme in one mode (Korak Newmarkove sheme v enem načinu)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C = \mat 0\), \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), \(\beta \ge 0\), \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\) and \(D = 1 + \beta\Omega^2\). For the Newmark scheme (definition 17.36) we have

\[\begin{pmatrix}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1} \\ p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1}\end{pmatrix} = \mat A\begin{pmatrix}\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} \\ p_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat A = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{1 - (\frac12 - \beta)\Omega^2}{D} & \dfrac{\Omega}{D} \\[2mm] -\Omega(1 - \gamma) - \gamma\Omega A_{11} & 1 - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}\end{pmatrix} , \tag{17.35}\]

where \(A_{11}\) is the element at the top left, and

\[\operatorname{tr}\mat A = 2 - \frac{(\gamma + \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{D} , \qquad \det\mat A = 1 - \frac{(\gamma - \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{D} . \tag{17.36}\]
Proof

We show that equations (17.33) and (17.34) are written by modes with the matrix \(\mat A\), and then we compute the trace and the determinant.

  1. We multiply equations (17.33) and (17.34) by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\). As in step 1 of the proof of theorem 10.67, \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\). The first equation gives \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Omega\,p_{\mathrm{k}} - \Omega^2\big((\tfrac12 - \beta)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \beta\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\), the second after division by \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) gives \(p_{\mathrm{k}+1} = p_{\mathrm{k}} - \Omega\big((1 - \gamma)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \gamma\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\) (we drop the index \(r\)).
  2. We solve the first equation for \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\): \(D\,\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \big(1 - (\tfrac12 - \beta)\Omega^2\big)\eta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Omega\,p_{\mathrm{k}}\). This is the first row of matrix (17.35).
  3. We insert \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) into the second equation. The coefficient of \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(-\Omega(1 - \gamma) - \gamma\Omega A_{11}\), and that of \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(1 - \gamma\Omega\cdot\Omega/D\). This is the second row.
  4. Trace: \(A_{11} + A_{22} = \dfrac{1 - (\frac12 - \beta)\Omega^2 + D - \gamma\Omega^2}{D} = \dfrac{2 + (2\beta - \frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2}{D}\). Since \(2D = 2 + 2\beta\Omega^2\), this is \(2 - (\gamma + \frac12)\Omega^2/D\).
  5. Determinant: \(A_{11}A_{22} - A_{12}A_{21}\). The product \(A_{12}A_{21} = -\dfrac{\Omega^2(1 - \gamma)}{D} - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}A_{11}\), and the product \(A_{11}A_{22} = A_{11} - \dfrac{\gamma\Omega^2}{D}A_{11}\). The terms with \(\gamma\Omega^2A_{11}/D\) cancel in the subtraction and what remains is \(\det\mat A = A_{11} + \dfrac{\Omega^2(1 - \gamma)}{D} = \dfrac{1 + (\frac12 + \beta - \gamma)\Omega^2}{D}\). Since \(D + (\frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2 = 1 + (\beta + \frac12 - \gamma)\Omega^2\), this is \(1 - (\gamma - \frac12)\Omega^2/D\).

Source: COOK §11.14 (PDF pp. 437 to 439) analyses the same with one mode and the roots of the characteristic equation. Equations (17.35) and (17.36) are ours (SymPy, outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-08.py, part S1, which checks both differences against zero).

The trace and the determinant fix the eigenvalues. For the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\)) the determinant is \(1\) and the eigenvalues are \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\,2\arctan(\Omega/2)}\) by theorem 10.67. What does a determinant that is not \(1\) do? The eigenvalues are conjugate numbers \(\lambda = \rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) and their product is \(\rho^2 = \det\mat A\). As point 2 of the theorem below shows, every step therefore multiplies the size of the oscillation by \(\rho\) and shifts its phase by \(\varphi\). At \(\det\mat A < 1\) the oscillation decays, at \(\det\mat A > 1\) it grows. The eigenvalues, however, are not necessarily conjugate: for a positive discriminant \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 - 4\det\mat A\) they are real, and then one of them can exceed \(1\) in absolute value even when \(\det\mat A < 1\). At \(\beta = (\gamma + \frac12)^2/4\) this cannot happen, as the theorem shows.

Theorem 17.39 Stability of the Newmark scheme at \(\beta = (\gamma + \frac12)^2/4\) (Stabilnost Newmarkove sheme)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C = \mat 0\), \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), \(\gamma\) a real number and \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\). For every mode \(r\) and every \(\Delta t > 0\) with \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\):

  1. The discriminant of the matrix \(\mat A\) of lemma 17.38 is \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 - 4\det\mat A = -4\Omega^2/D^2 < 0\), so the eigenvalues are conjugate numbers \(\rho\,\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\varphi}\) with \(\varphi \in (0, \pi)\) and
    \[\rho(\mat A)^2 = \det\mat A = 1 - \frac{(\gamma - \frac12)\,\Omega^2}{1 + \beta\,\Omega^2} . \tag{17.37}\]
  2. For every start there are numbers \(R\) and \(\delta\) such that \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = R\,\rho^k\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\) for every \(k \ge 0\). At \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) we therefore have \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \le R\) for every \(k\), and the scheme is unconditionally stable in the sense of definition 10.65.
  3. At \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho > 1\) at every \(\Omega > 0\), and the scheme is not stable at any step.
  4. The point \((\gamma, \beta)\) lies in the region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) of figure 17.23 exactly when \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\).
Proof

We show that the conjugate eigenvalues have the product \(\rho^2\) and that the recursion of lemma 10.69 then describes every mode.

  1. With \(g = \gamma + \tfrac12\) we have \(\beta = g^2/4\), so \(4\beta\Omega^2 = g^2\Omega^2 = 4(D - 1)\). By equation (17.36), \(\operatorname{tr}\mat A = 2 - g\Omega^2/D\) and \(\det\mat A = 1 - (g - 1)\Omega^2/D\). The discriminant is \(\big(2 - \tfrac{g\Omega^2}{D}\big)^2 - 4\big(1 - \tfrac{(g - 1)\Omega^2}{D}\big) = -\tfrac{4\Omega^2}{D} + \tfrac{g^2\Omega^4}{D^2} = \tfrac{\Omega^2}{D^2}\big(g^2\Omega^2 - 4D\big)\). Since \(g^2\Omega^2 = 4D - 4\), this is \(-4\Omega^2/D^2 < 0\). Hence \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 < 4\det\mat A\), so \(\det\mat A > 0\) and the eigenvalues are conjugate numbers with nonzero imaginary part. Their product is \(|\lambda|^2 = \rho^2 = \det\mat A\), which gives equation (17.37). The angle \(\varphi \in (0, \pi)\) is the angle of the eigenvalue with positive imaginary part, \(\cos\varphi = \operatorname{tr}\mat A/(2\rho)\).
  2. For a matrix with two rows, \(\mat A^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,\mat A + (\det\mat A)\,\mat I = \mat 0\) (direct multiplication of the elements). We apply this identity to the column \((\eta_{\mathrm{k}-1}, p_{\mathrm{k}-1})^\T\): for \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}}\) and also for \(p_{\mathrm{k}}\) we get \(u_{\mathrm{k}+1} - (\operatorname{tr}\mat A)\,u_{\mathrm{k}} + \rho^2\,u_{\mathrm{k}-1} = 0\) at \(k \ge 1\). With \(u_{\mathrm{k}} = \rho^k w_{\mathrm{k}}\) and division by \(\rho^{k+1}\) we get \(w_{\mathrm{k}+1} - 2b\,w_{\mathrm{k}} + w_{\mathrm{k}-1} = 0\) with \(b = \operatorname{tr}\mat A/(2\rho)\) and \(|b| < 1\), because \((\operatorname{tr}\mat A)^2 < 4\rho^2\). By point 1 of lemma 10.69, \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = w_0\cos k\psi + c\sin k\psi\) with \(\cos\psi = b\) and \(\psi \in (0, \pi)\), so \(\psi = \varphi\). With \(w_0\cos k\varphi + c\sin k\varphi = R\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\) and \(R = \sqrt{w_0^2 + c^2}\) we get \(\eta_{\mathrm{k}} = R\rho^k\cos(k\varphi - \delta)\).
  3. At \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) equation (17.37) gives \(\rho \le 1\), so \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \le R_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r\) and every \(k\). By corollary 10.14, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \eta_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{k}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), and by \(\mat M\)-orthonormality \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\eta_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{k}}^2 \le \sum_{\mathrm{s}} R_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). This is the bound \(B\) of definition 10.65 and it does not depend on \(k\). At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho = 1\), the amplitude is constant (as after theorem 10.66).
  4. Point 3. At \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\det\mat A > 1\), so \(\rho > 1\). Start with \(\vek q_0 = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek v_0 = \vek 0\), so \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},0} = 1\), \(p_{\mathrm{r},0} = 0\), and \(R \ge 1\). If \(\cos(k\varphi - \delta) \to 0\), then \(|\sin(k\varphi - \delta)| \to 1\) and \(\cos((k+1)\varphi - \delta) = \cos(k\varphi - \delta)\cos\varphi - \sin(k\varphi - \delta)\sin\varphi\) would have an absolute value tending to \(\sin\varphi \ne 0\), which is a contradiction. Hence \(|\cos(k\varphi - \delta)| \ge \varepsilon > 0\) for infinitely many \(k\), and \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}| \ge R\rho^k\varepsilon\) is not bounded. Since \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \ge \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}^2\), the scheme is not stable by definition 10.65.
  5. Point 4. From \(\beta - \gamma/2 = (\gamma - \tfrac12)^2/4 \ge 0\) we have \(2\beta \ge \gamma\) at every \(\gamma\), so the condition \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) is the same as \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433), (11.13-7): unconditional stability at \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\), stated there without proof, with a reference to the literature. The choice \(\beta = \tfrac14(\gamma + \tfrac12)^2\) is COOK (11.13-10), PDF p. 434: the best damping of high frequencies while unconditional stability is kept. The proof for this line, the splitting by modes and the recursion are ours. The general region of (11.13-7) is not proved here.

Point 2 of the theorem is what we obtained for the trapezoidal rule from one complex number: the size of the oscillation in mode \(r\) is multiplied by \(\rho\) after every step and the phase is turned by \(\varphi\). At \(\gamma = \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho = 1\), at \(\gamma > \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho < 1\), at \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) we have \(\rho > 1\). This is not conditional stability as with central differences. The scheme at \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) inflates every oscillation at every step.

Definition 17.40 Numerical damping (Numerično dušenje)

Let the Newmark scheme at \(\mat C = \mat 0\) satisfy theorem 17.39 and let \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho(\mat A)\) be the spectral radius of the step in mode \(r\) at \(\Omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\). The scheme has numerical damping (numerično dušenje, in COOK algorithmic damping) in mode \(r\) if \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}} < 1\). The number

\[\zeta_{\mathrm{num},\mathrm{r}} = -\frac{\ln\rho_{\mathrm{r}}}{\Omega_{\mathrm{r}}} \tag{17.38}\]

is the numerical damping ratio of mode \(r\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433 to 434): "algorithmic damping", at \(\gamma > \tfrac12\). The ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{num}}\) is ours: the reason is that viscous damping with ratio \(\zeta\) reduces the size of a mode after time \(\Delta t\) by \(\mathrm{e}^{-\zeta\omega\Delta t}\) (section 10.9.2), and the scheme after one step by \(\rho_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is the same at \(\zeta = \zeta_{\mathrm{num},\mathrm{r}}\).

The name says that the damping does not come from the structure but from the computing procedure: it is not in the matrix \(\mat C\) and we cannot assign it to any mechanism. The damping that comes from the structure is treated in chapter 20.

Corollary 17.41 Numerical damping of high and low modes (Numerično dušenje visokih in nizkih načinov)

Let \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\) and \(\tfrac12 < \gamma \le \tfrac32\). The spectral radius \(\rho(\mat A)\) of equation (17.37) is a decreasing function of the number \(\Omega\) with the limits

\[\rho(\mat A) \to 1 \ \ (\Omega \to 0) , \qquad \rho(\mat A) \to \frac{\tfrac32 - \gamma}{\gamma + \tfrac12} \ \ (\Omega \to \infty) . \tag{17.39}\]

At small \(\Omega\) we have \(\rho(\mat A)^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\,\Omega^2 + O(\Omega^4)\).

Proof

We show that the fraction \(h(\Omega) = \Omega^2/(1 + \beta\Omega^2)\) in equation (17.37) is increasing and has the limit \(1/\beta\).

  1. We have \(h = \tfrac1\beta\big(1 - \tfrac{1}{1 + \beta\Omega^2}\big)\). The fraction \(1/(1 + \beta\Omega^2)\) decreases with \(\Omega\) towards \(0\), so \(h\) increases from \(0\) towards \(1/\beta\).
  2. Hence \(\rho^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\,h\) decreases from \(1\) towards \(1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)/\beta = 1 - \dfrac{4(\gamma - \frac12)}{(\gamma + \frac12)^2}\). Since \((\gamma + \tfrac12)^2 - 4\gamma + 2 = \gamma^2 - 3\gamma + \tfrac94 = (\gamma - \tfrac32)^2\), this limit is \(\dfrac{(\gamma - \frac32)^2}{(\gamma + \frac12)^2}\), so the limit of \(\rho\) is \((\tfrac32 - \gamma)/(\gamma + \tfrac12)\) at \(\gamma \le \tfrac32\).
  3. Expansion: \(h = \Omega^2 - \beta\Omega^4 + \dots\) (the series for \(1/(1 + s)\) with remainder \(s^2/(1+s)\), \(s = \beta\Omega^2\)), from which \(\rho^2 = 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\Omega^2 + O(\Omega^4)\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 433 to 434): "when \(\gamma > \tfrac12\), Newmark methods display algorithmic damping, at the cost of reducing guaranteed accuracy from second-order to first-order", and the choice (11.13-10). The limit at \(\Omega \to \infty\) and the expansion are not in the source. The proof is ours (SymPy, num-08.py, parts S1 and S2).

The expansion also tells why COOK says that damping costs one order of accuracy. The size is multiplied in every step by \(\rho \approx 1 - (\gamma - \tfrac12)\Omega^2/2\) (from \(\sqrt{1 - x} \approx 1 - x/2\) at small \(x\)), and there are about \(2\pi/\Omega\) steps per oscillation, so the size after one oscillation falls by about \(\pi(\gamma - \tfrac12)\,\Omega\). This loss is proportional to \(\Omega\), that is to the step \(\Delta t\) in the first power, and is therefore of first order. At the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\)) the loss is zero, and the second order stays in the phase (theorem 10.67).

Example 17.42 How much the amplitude is reduced (Koliko se zmanjša obseg)

A mode with \(\Omega = 2\pi/20 = 0{,}31416\), that is \(20\) steps per oscillation, has at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) (\(\beta = 0{,}3025\)) the spectral radius \(0{,}99520\) and after \(20\) steps the size \(0{,}99520^{20} = 0{,}9082\) of the initial one. The numerical damping ratio by equation (17.38) is \(0{,}01533\). At \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) (\(\beta = 0{,}36\)) we have \(\rho = 0{,}99042\), the size after \(20\) steps \(0{,}8249\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{num}} = 0{,}03063\). The same mode with the same step loses nothing at the trapezoidal rule. A mode with \(\Omega = 10\), that is \(0{,}63\) steps per oscillation, has at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) after one step \(0{,}82462\) and \(0{,}67783\) of the previous size, and at \(\Omega = 1000\) it has \(0{,}81818\) and \(0{,}66667\), which are the limits \((\tfrac32 - \gamma)/(\gamma + \tfrac12)\) of equation (17.39). The values are in the table (NumPy, num-08.py, part S2).

\(\omega\Delta t\) \(0{,}1\) \(2\pi/20\) \(1\) \(10\) \(1000\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}5\), \(\beta = 0{,}25\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\) \(1{,}00000\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}6\), \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) \(0{,}99950\) \(0{,}99520\) \(0{,}96085\) \(0{,}82462\) \(0{,}81818\)
\(\gamma = 0{,}7\), \(\beta = 0{,}36\) \(0{,}99900\) \(0{,}99042\) \(0{,}92355\) \(0{,}67783\) \(0{,}66667\)

Figure 17.24 shows the same numbers. We draw the horizontal axis \(\omega\Delta t\) on a logarithmic scale and the vertical axis \(\rho(\mat A)\). The scale is logarithmic because we care about modes from an oscillation with several hundred steps to an oscillation with a part of a step, which is a range of several orders of magnitude. The trapezoidal rule gives a horizontal line at \(1\): it damps no mode. The curve \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) lies on \(1\) at small \(\omega\Delta t\), falls around \(\omega\Delta t \approx 2\) and settles at the dashed limit \(0{,}818\). The curve \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) falls lower and settles at \(0{,}667\). The vertical line at \(2\pi/20\) is the case of the example above, where the curves cut the line in the dots at \(0{,}995\) and \(0{,}990\).

Why damp at all? The highest modes of a mesh have frequencies that are poorly determined: the order of the error from corollary 10.38 holds at fixed \(r\) and falling \(h\), not for the highest modes of the mesh. These modes are often not part of what we care about, and boundary conditions or a sudden load can excite them. COOK gives this as the reason for numerical damping: to damp high modes that are "of little interest or constitute only undesirable nonphysical oscillations associated with discretization" (COOK PDF p. 434). Adding viscous damping raises \(\zeta\), but according to Hughes, whom COOK cites, with the trapezoidal rule it may damp mostly the middle modes, while the highest and the lowest stay almost untouched (COOK PDF p. 434). Numerical damping with the curves of figure 17.24 is therefore the better choice: it damps the more the higher the frequency.

The figure also shows the price. At \(\gamma = 0{,}7\) a mode with \(20\) steps per oscillation is reduced to \(82{,}5\) % in one oscillation, which is about a damping ratio of \(3\) %, and this is not in the model. Whoever compares the measured damping of a structure with the response of a computation with \(\gamma > \tfrac12\) compares the measured value with only a part of the computed damping. For this reason \(\gamma\) is kept near \(\tfrac12\), and at \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) the damping is \(1{,}5\) %. COOK also names the \(\alpha\)-method (Hilber, Hughes and Taylor), which keeps the damping in high modes and reduces it in low ones, without losing the second order (COOK PDF p. 433 to 434). That scheme is only named here. The opposite direction is more dangerous still: at \(\gamma = 0{,}4\) (\(\beta = 0{,}2025\)) we have \(\rho > 1\) by theorem 17.39, point 3, and a mode with \(\Omega = 2\pi/20\) grows after \(20\) steps to \(1{,}1011\) of its size, and at \(\Omega = 10\) by a factor \(1{,}2127\) per step (num-08.py, part S5). A scheme with \(\gamma < \tfrac12\) is therefore not inaccurate but wrong.

17.8.3 The nonlinear step (Nelinearni korak)

So far the force was linear, \(\mat K\vek q\). A nonlinear system has an internal force \(\vek f(\vek q)\) that is no longer linear, and the equation of motion \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \vek f(\vek q) = \vek Q(t)\) (a conservative system without damping). For \(\vek f = \mat K\vek q\) we get the previous equation. The Newmark equations (17.33) and (17.34) stay, because they speak only of displacement, velocity and acceleration. At \(\beta > 0\) we express from the first the acceleration at the end of the step through the unknown \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\),

\[\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} - \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} - \Delta t^2(\frac12 - \beta)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}}{\beta\,\Delta t^2} , \tag{17.40}\]

and insert it in the equation of motion at the end of the step. An equation for one unknown remains, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\),

\[\vek G(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = \mat M\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) + \vek f(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek 0 . \tag{17.41}\]

For a linear \(\vek f = \mat K\vek q\) this is a linear equation with the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}} = \mat K + \mat M/(\beta\Delta t^2)\), and at \(\beta = \tfrac14\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\) it is exactly equation (10.77). In the nonlinear case we solve it with Newton's method from section 17.7 (definition 17.32): from an approximation \(\vek q^{(i)}\) we get the next one with

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)}\,\Delta\vek q = -\vek G\big(\vek q^{(i)}\big) , \qquad \mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)} = \mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\big(\vek q^{(i)}\big) + \frac{\mat M}{\beta\,\Delta t^2} , \tag{17.42}\]
