where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the tangent stiffness (definition 17.31) and \(\Delta\vek q\) the correction of the approximation. We start with the approximation from the start of the step, \(\vek q^{(0)} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t^2(\tfrac12 - \beta)\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\), that is with the displacement that equation (17.33) would give at \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek 0\). A warning about the cost: the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}^{(i)}\) changes with \(\vek q^{(i)}\), so the factorization of the matrix (lemma 7.47), which we did once for all steps in the linear system (chapter 10), is repeated here at every iteration of every step. This is the cost of nonlinearity (section 17.6 treats large systems). We stop the iterations when the correction is smaller than \(\delta\) (section 17.7), and this stopping is the numerical error of definition 17.2.

Does equation (17.41) have a solution at all, and one only? We show this on the pendulum, where the unknown is one angle.

Lemma 17.43 The step equation for the pendulum (Enačba koraka za nihalo)

Let the pendulum (\(\ddot\theta = -\sin\theta\), time in units of \(\sqrt{l/g}\)) make a step \(\Delta t\) with the trapezoidal rule (\(\gamma = \tfrac12\), \(\beta = \tfrac14\)) from the state \((\theta_{\mathrm{k}}, v_{\mathrm{k}}, a_{\mathrm{k}})\). The equation for \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is \(g(\theta) = \theta - c + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\sin\theta = 0\) with \(c = \theta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}a_{\mathrm{k}}\). At \(\Delta t < 2\) it has exactly one solution. At \(\Delta t > 2\) there may be more solutions.

Proof

We show that at \(\Delta t < 2\) the function \(g\) is strictly increasing and unbounded in both directions, and that this does not hold for a larger step.

  1. From equation (17.40) at \(\beta = \tfrac14\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = -\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) it follows that \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \theta_{\mathrm{k}} + \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\big(a_{\mathrm{k}} - \sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\big)\), which is \(g(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = 0\).
  2. The derivative is \(g'(\theta) = 1 + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\cos\theta \ge 1 - \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\). At \(\Delta t < 2\) this is a positive number, so \(g\) is strictly increasing (mean value theorem).
  3. Since \(|\sin\theta| \le 1\), we have \(g(\theta) \ge \theta - c - \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\) and \(g(\theta) \le \theta - c + \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{4}\). So \(g < 0\) at small enough and \(g > 0\) at large enough \(\theta\). A continuous, strictly increasing function that changes sign has by the intermediate value theorem exactly one zero.
  4. At \(\Delta t > 2\) we have \(g'(\theta) < 0\) where \(\cos\theta < -4/\Delta t^2\), so \(g\) is not monotonic and may have several zeros. An example is in the example below.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

An example with numbers. The pendulum from the position \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}} = \pi/2\) with \(v_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) and \(a_{\mathrm{k}} = -1\) has \(c = \pi/2 - \Delta t^2/4\). Figure 17.25 shows the function \(g\). We draw the axis \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and the axis \(g\), where a zero means a solution. At \(\Delta t = 2\pi/20 = 0{,}31416\) we have \(g' \ge 0{,}9753\), the blue curve is almost a straight line and has one zero at \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1} = 1{,}5215\). At \(\Delta t = 4\) it is no longer monotonic: the orange curve has three zeros at \(-5{,}4335\), \(-3{,}3821\) and \(-0{,}5026\) (num-08.py, part S5). The step \(\Delta t = 4\) is useless for computing the oscillation, since the period at small deflections is \(2\pi \approx 6{,}28\), fewer than two steps per oscillation, but it shows that unconditional stability in the linear case is not a property of the scheme on the nonlinear equation: there the step is not even uniquely determined. What matters most to us is that at this step Newton's method finds one of the three zeros, depending on the initial approximation, and not necessarily the one we want. Similarly, in section 17.7 at a load above the limit force it found an equilibrium that is not stable.

17.8.4 The pendulum (Nihalo)

The model is a point mass on a rigid weightless rod of length \(l\) in the gravity field \(g\) with the angle \(\theta\) from the vertical, without friction in the axis and without air drag. The equation of motion is \(\ddot\theta = -(g/l)\sin\theta\) (theorem 8.123). For time we take the unit \(\sqrt{l/g}\), and the equation is \(\theta'' + \sin\theta = 0\) (the prime is the derivative with respect to dimensionless time). This is equation (17.41) with \(M = 1\), \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta\), \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = \cos\theta\) and \(Q = 0\). We start from \(\theta_0 = \pi/2\), \(v_0 = 0\) and use the trapezoidal rule with Newton at every step. By theorem 8.123 the exact period at amplitude \(90°\) is \(T = 4\int_0^{\pi/2}\big(1 - \tfrac12\sin^2u\big)^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u = 7{,}41630\) (NumPy, arithmetic-geometric mean), at small amplitude \(2\pi = 6{,}28319\). At \(l = 1\) m and \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s\(^2\) the unit of time is \(0{,}3193\) s, and \(T = 2{,}368\) s.

Figure 17.26 shows three oscillations. We draw the time axis and the axis of deflection \(\theta\) with the limits \(\pm\pi/2\). The grey curve is the exact solution, computed with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method with the step \(3T/20000 \approx 0{,}0011\), about \(565\) times smaller than the step of the scheme (fig-08.py), so the difference is zero to the accuracy of drawing. The blue dots are the values of the trapezoidal rule with step \(2\pi/10\), which is deliberately coarse here so that the error is visible. The dots lag behind the curve: the scheme slows the pendulum down. The cause is already known from theorem 10.67: the trapezoidal rule turns the phase by \(2\arctan(\Omega/2)\) instead of \(\Omega\), and the period in the scheme is therefore longer. The pendulum at amplitude \(90°\) has a frequency lower than \(1\), namely \(2\pi/T = 0{,}84721\). With it \(x = 0{,}84721\cdot 2\pi/20/2 = 0{,}13308\) and \(x/\arctan x - 1 = 0{,}588\) %, which is close to the measured \(0{,}57\) % at step \(2\pi/20\). The linear formula of chapter 10 therefore predicts the error well also for the nonlinear pendulum (table below).

The results with three smaller steps are in the table. At every step Newton needed at most \(3\) iterations (\(4\) at \(\Delta t = 2\pi/10\)), stopping at a correction below \(10^{-12}\). The last column is the largest deviation of the energy \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12v_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + 1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) from the initial value \(\mathcal{E}_0 = 1\) in three oscillations.

\(\Delta t\) period error iterations per step \(\max\lvert\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} - 1\rvert\)
\(2\pi/10\) \(7{,}58203\) \(2{,}23\) % \(4\) \(3{,}05\cdot 10^{-2}\)
\(2\pi/20\) \(7{,}45854\) \(0{,}57\) % \(3\) \(8{,}06\cdot 10^{-3}\)
\(2\pi/40\) \(7{,}42673\) \(0{,}14\) % \(3\) \(2{,}05\cdot 10^{-3}\)
\(2\pi/80\) \(7{,}41890\) \(0{,}04\) % \(3\) \(5{,}13\cdot 10^{-4}\)

The error of the period falls about four times when the step is halved, which is second order. The same holds for the energy. In a linear system the trapezoidal rule conserves the energy exactly (theorem 10.66). For the pendulum it does not, and not because of rounding: even the smallest difference in the table, \(5{,}13\cdot 10^{-4}\), is more than ten orders of magnitude above rounding, which is about \(10^{-16}\). Why is shown by a computation that repeats the proof of theorem 10.66 and stops where the force is no longer linear. We do it for a general force \(f\) and one degree of freedom.

Theorem 17.44 Energy of the trapezoidal rule for a nonlinear force (Energija trapeznega pravila pri nelinearni sili)

Let \(f\) be a twice continuously differentiable function, \(V\) its antiderivative (\(V' = f\)), \(\ddot q + f(q) = 0\) the equation of motion of unit mass, and let the trapezoidal rule (definition 10.63) with step \(\Delta t\) give the sequence \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{k}} = -f(q_{\mathrm{k}})\). With \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12v_{\mathrm{k}}^2 + V(q_{\mathrm{k}})\) and \(h_{\mathrm{k}} = q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - q_{\mathrm{k}}\) we have

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \int_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{k}}^{q_{\mathrm{k}+1}}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s - \frac{h_{\mathrm{k}}}{2}\big(f(q_{\mathrm{k}}) + f(q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\big) , \tag{17.43}\]

and this difference is in absolute value at most \(\dfrac{\lvert h_{\mathrm{k}}\rvert^3}{12}\max\lvert f''\rvert\), where the maximum is over the interval between \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). For a linear \(f\) the difference is zero.

Proof

We show that the increment of energy is the error of the trapezoidal formula for the integral of the force.

  1. Kinetic part: \(\tfrac12(v_{\mathrm{k}+1}^2 - v_{\mathrm{k}}^2) = \tfrac12(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + v_{\mathrm{k}})(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - v_{\mathrm{k}})\). By equation (10.75) we have \(v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - v_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(a_{\mathrm{k}} + a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\), and by equation (10.74) \(\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(v_{\mathrm{k}} + v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = h_{\mathrm{k}}\). So the kinetic part is \(\tfrac12h_{\mathrm{k}}(a_{\mathrm{k}} + a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = -\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}}{2}\big(f(q_{\mathrm{k}}) + f(q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\big)\).
  2. Potential part: \(V(q_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - V(q_{\mathrm{k}}) = \int_{\mathrm{q}_\mathrm{k}}^{q_{\mathrm{k}+1}}f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The sum of steps 1 and 2 is equation (17.43).
  3. Let \(a < b\) be the end points of the interval. Integration by parts twice gives \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b(s - a)(b - s)f''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = (b - a)\big(f(a) + f(b)\big) - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\): the first boundary term \((s - a)(b - s)f'\) is zero at the end points, and the second part gives \(-\big[(a + b - 2s)f\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf\), which is \((b - a)(f(a) + f(b)) - 2\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf\).
  4. Hence \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^bf - \tfrac{b - a}{2}(f(a) + f(b)) = -\tfrac12\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b(s - a)(b - s)f''(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The kernel \((s - a)(b - s)\) is non-negative with integral \((b - a)^3/6\), so the absolute value of the right side is at most \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{(b - a)^3}{6}\max|f''| = \tfrac{(b - a)^3}{12}\max|f''|\). At \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) we swap the meaning of the end points and the expression for the difference gets the opposite sign, the absolute value stays. For a linear \(f\) we have \(f'' = 0\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. For a linear force it condenses theorem 10.66. The error of the trapezoidal formula is mentioned in COOK (PDF p. 619) only as second order (parameter \(0{,}5\) in the generalized trapezoidal formula (17.3-8)).

For the pendulum \(f = \sin\), \(|f''| \le 1\) and every step changes the energy by at most \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}|^3/12\). This is an upper bound for a single step. The sum of these bounds over three oscillations is \(0{,}708\), \(0{,}192\), \(0{,}049\) and \(0{,}0123\) at the four steps of the table, so it indeed falls four times with every halved step, because \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}| \approx \Delta t\,|v_{\mathrm{k}}|\) and \(|h_{\mathrm{k}}|^3\approx\Delta t^3|v_{\mathrm{k}}|^3\) at \(\sim\!1/\Delta t\) steps. But the bound is too loose, since the actual deviation is \(8{,}06\cdot 10^{-3}\) and not \(0{,}192\). The signs cancel, as figure 17.27 shows. We draw the time axis and the axis of the difference \(\mathcal{E} - \mathcal{E}_0\). At step \(2\pi/20\) (blue) the difference is everywhere negative or near zero, reaches \(-0{,}0081\) at the passage through the lowest position and returns to zero at every turning point: the energy therefore does not drift away but oscillates around the true value at the bottom. The steps \(2\pi/40\) (orange) and \(2\pi/80\) (grey) give the same shape four and sixteen times smaller.

Why does it return to zero? By theorem 17.44 the increment is \(-\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}^3}{12}f''(\xi_{\mathrm{k}})\) with \(f'' = -\sin\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{k}}\) between \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), so approximately \(+\tfrac{h_{\mathrm{k}}^3}{12}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\) (this is an estimate, not a theorem: we replace \(\xi_{\mathrm{k}}\) by \(\theta_{\mathrm{k}}\)). On the way from \(\theta = \pi/2\) towards \(0\) we have \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) and \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\), so the increment is negative. On the way from \(0\) towards \(-\pi/2\) we have \(h_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\) and \(\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}} < 0\), so the increment is positive. We add the first part as a Riemann sum with step \(\Delta t\) and \(h_{\mathrm{k}} \approx \Delta t\,v_{\mathrm{k}}\): \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} h_{\mathrm{k}}^3\sin\theta_{\mathrm{k}}/12 \approx \tfrac{\Delta t^2}{12}\int_0^{T/4}v^3\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}t\). For the exact solution, conservation of energy gives \(v^2 = 2\cos\theta\), and with the substitution \(\theta = \theta(t)\), for which \(\theta'(t) = v(t)\), the integral is \(\int_{\pi/2}^{0}2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -1\) (NumPy, \(40000\) steps: \(-1{,}00000\)). The deviation at the bottom is therefore about \(-\Delta t^2/12 = -0{,}0833\,\Delta t^2\), and the measured values are \(0{,}0817\), \(0{,}0829\) and \(0{,}0832\) times \(\Delta t^2\). The second part of the oscillation brings the same value with the opposite sign, so the energy returns at the turning points.

Such arguments are estimates and not proofs, and the book claims no more than the computation shows: we proved theorem 17.44 (the energy error per step), the quadratic order of the total error we estimated and checked at four steps. For the pendulum \(\max|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} - \mathcal{E}_0|\) is small, but the pendulum is a single mode. In a system with many modes the energy error of every mode is different, and nonlinearity couples them, which this section does not treat.

Example 17.45 An explicit step and a growing stiffness (Eksplicitni korak in rastoča togost)

The unconditional stability of the trapezoidal rule is a property of the linear mode (theorem 17.39). Explicit central differences have the critical step \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 2/\omega_{\max}\) (theorem 10.70), where \(\omega_{\max}\) is the highest frequency of the system. For a nonlinear force the leading stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) depends on the displacement, so \(\omega_{\max}\) depends on it too. Take the hardening spring \(\ddot q + q + 100\,q^3 = 0\) with \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = 1 + 300\,q^2\). At \(q = 0\) we have \(\omega_{\max} = 1\) and \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 2\). At \(q = 1\) we have \(\omega_{\max} = \sqrt{301} = 17{,}35\) and \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}} = 0{,}1153\). We start from \(q_0 = 0\) with velocity \(v_0 = 7{,}14\), which has an amplitude around \(1\), and make \(400\) steps of central differences (num-08.py, part S4). At \(\Delta t = 0{,}02\), \(0{,}05\) and \(0{,}08\) the solution stays bounded with the largest deflection \(1{,}0016\), \(1{,}0120\) and \(1{,}0397\). At \(\Delta t = 0{,}1\) and \(0{,}13\) it exceeds \(10^6\) after \(17\) and \(23\) steps. The step \(0{,}1\) is below the critical step at amplitude \(1\), yet the solution escapes: the critical step holds for a given \(\omega_{\max}\), but the deflection in an explicit scheme grows because of inaccuracy to a value where \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) is smaller than the step. This is not a proof for every system, but it is an example of why explicit schemes for nonlinear systems need a reserve below the critical step computed with the largest expected deflection.

Figure 17.25 connected the step, the equation and Newton, and figure 17.27 the price we pay for nonlinearity. The section showed three things. In a linear mode the family \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\) keeps stability for every \(\gamma \ge \tfrac12\) (theorem 17.39), and the damping of high modes costs one order of accuracy, since the guaranteed accuracy falls from second to first order (corollary 17.41). In the nonlinear step we solve the equation for the unknown displacement with Newton's method, and for the pendulum the step is certainly unique at \(\Delta t < 2\) (lemma 17.43). The trapezoidal rule does not conserve energy for a nonlinear force, and the error per step is given by theorem 17.44. Three proofs (stability of the family, uniqueness of the step and the energy error) we made ourselves, three statements we gave without proof: unconditional stability in the whole region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\), conditional stability of the linear acceleration scheme and the second order of the \(\alpha\)-method (COOK PDF p. 430 to 434).

17.9 Planning an analysis and the tube case study

The earlier sections of this chapter gave the parts: what a model is (section 17.1), how a body becomes a model (section 17.2), how we check that a result settles down as the mesh is refined (section 17.3), what to do with stresses (section 17.4), when a mesh is bad (section 17.5) and when a system of equations is hard (section 17.6). Whoever carries out an analysis needs an order: what to decide before the first computation, what after it, and when to stop. We call this order the plan of an analysis (načrt analize). In everyday use a plan is a drawing or a sequence of work made before the building starts, and that is what it is here: the decisions we make before the computation so that the computation answers the question we asked.

The plan does not treat only one of the three errors of definition 17.2. It leads us through all three: modelling error (the model against the real body), discretization error (the finite element solution against the exact solution of the model) and numerical error (round-off and stopped iterations). Reducing one does not reduce the others, so the plan separates them and gives each its own step. The steps follow COOK §10.12 to §10.15 (PDF pp. 375-382) and ONATE1 §1.4.4 (PDF pp. 31-33). We test them on the tube of chapter 11, because we know its exact solution and can see what each step tells us and what it does not.

The model is this tube: steel, inner radius \(a = 40\) mm and outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), oil pressure \(p = 30\) MPa in the bore and a free outer surface (theorem 11.27). The idealizations are the same as there: the material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic, and the pressure is uniform over the bore. The ends of the tube are not fixed by the problem. Chapter 11 computed three possibilities, open ends, closed ends and plane strain (definition 11.30), and at \(p = 30\) MPa the von Mises stresses (definition 2.76) at the bore are \(96{,}56\), \(93{,}53\) and \(94{,}02\) MPa. The yield pressure \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) is the pressure at which this stress equals the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa of section 2.12.5 of chapter 2, so \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 30 \cdot 220/\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\). We carry out the task as if we did not know the exact solution, and compare with it at the end.

We build the figure step by step, as one solves the task. First the question: from it follows which quantity we compute and how accurately we need it. For the tube the question is when it starts to yield, and the quantity is the von Mises stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}(a)\) at the bore, because by chapter 11 it is largest there. We choose the accuracy ourselves, \(2\,\%\) for the example, because an error in \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) changes \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) by the same fraction. This is our choice for the example and not a datum from a source. For another task the requirement may differ, but it must be written down before the computation, since without it we do not know when the mesh is fine enough.

17.9.1 Question and hand estimate

The second step is the hand calculation, before we open the program. COOK demands it with a good reason: since we find it hard to give up a result that took much work, an approximate result should be ready beforehand, and even a rough calculation detects a displacement in the wrong direction, a strange shape of the field or an error of orders of magnitude (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 375). For the tube the calculation is already in section 11.7.1 of chapter 11. Half the tube per unit length is in equilibrium if the pressure resultant \(2\,p\,a\) equals the sum of the forces in the two cuts (figure 11.18), so

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = p\,a , \tag{17.44}\]

(equation (11.32)), and the mean hoop stress is \(p\,a/(b - a) = 60\) MPa. With the mean radius in place of \(a\) we get \(75\) MPa (equation (11.33)). The true value at the bore is known from theorem 11.27, \(78\) MPa, and the first two numbers are \(23\,\%\) and \(4\,\%\) below it. The hand calculation here gives the order of magnitude and the sign of the stress, not the stress to \(2\,\%\). Since the two numbers differ from each other by \(25\,\%\), it would catch a factor of \(10\) or a wrong sign, but not finer errors.

The hand calculation and the computer result must refer to the same physical case (COOK §10.15, PDF p. 381). If we compare \(78\) MPa with a mesh that has another pressure or another bore radius, the difference must not be put down to the mesh.

17.9.2 Sequence of models and meshes

The third step is the choice of model. COOK advises a sequence of models from simple to detailed, each correcting the faults of the previous one, because this is faster than one large model that turns out wrong when we look at its result (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 376). For the tube the sequence is: the thin-wall formula (step 2), the Lamé solution, and finally the finite element model. One question remains in the model, the ends of the tube. By theorem 11.27 the constants \(A\) and \(B\), and with them \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\), do not depend on the axial stress \(S\), which enters only \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\). So the mesh computes the same \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) for all three ends, and the difference of \(3{,}2\,\%\) between \(96{,}56\) and \(93{,}53\) MPa is wholly modelling error. The mesh does not reduce it (definition 17.2), only knowledge of how the tube is really closed decides it.

The computational model is the radial problem of the tube in plane strain with linear elements along the radius, as section 17.4 derives it from the weak form (lemma 17.17). The fourth step is a sequence of meshes with \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\) equal elements. Doubling is not arbitrary: theorem 17.14 needs three nested meshes, each differing from the previous one by the same factor. Example 17.46 collects the results.

Example 17.46 Tube at \(p = 30\) MPa, sequence of meshes (cev, zaporedje mrež)

The values at the inner edge \(r = a\) come from the element at the bore, the stresses from the displacements by Hooke's law, the axial stress from \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \nu\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta})\) (plane strain), and the exact values are \(u(a) = 16{,}8735\ \mu\)m and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = 94{,}02\) MPa. The error is the difference from the exact value in per cent of that value, and all errors are negative except the error of the hoop stress. The computation is in outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-09.py (NumPy).

\(n\) \(u(a)\) (\(\mu\)m) error of \(u(a)\) \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a)\) (MPa) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}(a)\) (MPa) error of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (MPa)
1 \(16{,}2265\) \(-3{,}834\,\%\) \(88{,}45\) \(76{,}61\) \(-18{,}52\,\%\) \(86{,}15\)
2 \(16{,}6928\) \(-1{,}071\,\%\) \(85{,}35\) \(84{,}41\) \(-10{,}22\,\%\) \(78{,}19\)
4 \(16{,}8268\) \(-0{,}276\,\%\) \(82{,}33\) \(88{,}92\) \(-5{,}42\,\%\) \(74{,}22\)
8 \(16{,}8617\) \(-0{,}070\,\%\) \(80{,}34\) \(91{,}39\) \(-2{,}80\,\%\) \(72{,}22\)
16 \(16{,}8705\) \(-0{,}017\,\%\) \(79{,}22\) \(92{,}68\) \(-1{,}43\,\%\) \(71{,}21\)
32 \(16{,}8727\) \(-0{,}004\,\%\) \(78{,}62\) \(93{,}34\) \(-0{,}72\,\%\) \(70{,}71\)

Figure 17.29 takes two columns of the table. First the axes: horizontally the number of elements \(n\) in doublings, vertically the error in per cent on a logarithmic scale, so a straight line means that the error falls as a power of the element size \(h \sim 1/n\). The blackwhite line is the error of the displacement \(u(a)\): at every doubling it falls to a quarter, which is second order, as section 17.3 predicts for displacements. The blue line is the error of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) at the bore and falls only to a half, so it is first order, because the stress is computed from the derivative of the displacements (section 17.4). The order observed from three consecutive meshes is \(0{,}93\) at \(n = 4, 8, 16\) and \(0{,}96\) at \(n = 8, 16, 32\). The horizontal dashed line at \(2\) is the chosen tolerance: the blue line crosses it between \(n = 8\) (\(2{,}80\,\%\)) and \(n = 16\) (\(1{,}43\,\%\)). The dashed line at \(0{,}53\) is the difference between plane strain and closed ends (\(94{,}02\) against \(93{,}53\) MPa, \(0{,}53\,\%\) of the second value). The blue line is still above it at \(n = 32\), at \(0{,}72\,\%\). The vertical dashed line at \(n = 16\) says one more thing: at this mesh the displacement at the bore is exact to \(0{,}017\,\%\) and the stress to \(1{,}43\,\%\), worse by a factor of \(82\) (from the unrounded errors \(1{,}427\,\%\) and \(0{,}0175\,\%\)). COOK writes this as advice to use a finer mesh for stresses than for displacements (COOK §10.12, PDF p. 376), and the table shows how much finer.

The error has a sign. All the values of \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}}\) from the mesh are below the exact one, so the yield pressure \(p_{\mathrm{Y}}\) computed from them is above the true one: at \(n = 16\) it is \(71{,}21\) against \(70{,}20\) MPa. For the question about yielding this is an error on the unsafe side, which is the reason not to stop the mesh at the first number that is close.

17.9.3 Checks and mistakes

The fifth step is the checks of the result. Section 7.10.2 of chapter 7 collected eight of them. For the truss the first is the sum of reactions that balances the load (lemma 7.20). The tube has no supports, so its equivalent check is in half the tube: for the exact field equation (17.44) holds. Does the solution from the mesh satisfy it too?

Lemma 17.47 Half-tube equilibrium for the finite element solution (ravnovesje polovice cevi pri rešitvi iz mreže)

Let \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) be the solution of the radial problem of the tube \(a \le r \le b\) of lemma 17.17 on a mesh \(a = r_0 < r_1 < \dots < r_{\mathrm{n}} = b\) with hat functions \(\psi_0, \dots, \psi_{\mathrm{n}}\) (definition 6.25), all nodes free, pressure \(p_{\mathrm{a}}\) at \(r = a\) and a free outer surface. Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}\) be the stresses from \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) by Hooke's law of plane strain at the Gauss point \(g\), and \(w_{\mathrm{g}} = h_{\mathrm{e}}/2\) the weight of the two-point Gauss rule (definition 7.24) in the element \(e\) of length \(h_{\mathrm{e}}\). Let the system matrix be computed with the same rule, as in the computation of example 17.46. Then for every mesh

\[\sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}} = p_{\mathrm{a}}\,a , \tag{17.45}\]

the sum running over all Gauss points of all elements.

Proof

We show that the sum of the rows of the system of equations for \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) gives exactly equation (17.45).

  1. The system is \(K\,\vek d = \vek f\) with \(f_0 = p_{\mathrm{a}} a\) and \(f_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(i \ge 1\) (lemma 17.17: the work of the pressure on a virtual displacement \(v\) is \(p_{\mathrm{a}} a\,v(a)\), and the hat function \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is one only at node \(i\)). By hypothesis the matrix is a sum over Gauss points, \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,r_{\mathrm{g}}\,\big(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'(r_{\mathrm{g}})\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}] + \psi_{\mathrm{i}}(r_{\mathrm{g}})\,\sigma_{\theta\theta}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]/r_{\mathrm{g}}\big)\), where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}[\psi_{\mathrm{j}}]\) are the stresses of the field \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\). By linearity, \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{ij}} d_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,r_{\mathrm{g}}\,\big(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}} + \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\big)\).
  2. On every element only two hat functions are nonzero, both linear with sum \(1\) (definition 6.25), so \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^{n}\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = 1\) on the whole interval and \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}' = 0\).
  3. We add the equations for \(i = 0, \dots, n\). By step 2 the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr},\mathrm{g}}\) is zero, the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\) is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}/r_{\mathrm{g}}\), and the factor \(r_{\mathrm{g}}\) cancels. The left side is \(\sum_{\mathrm{g}} w_{\mathrm{g}}\,\sigma_{\theta\theta,\mathrm{g}}\).
  4. The right side of the sum is \(f_0 = p_{\mathrm{a}} a\). Equating gives equation (17.45). \(\square\)

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The check follows the sum of reactions: COOK §10.15 (PDF p. 381).

The lemma says more than it seems. The sum is the Gauss sum for \(\int\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r\), so the mesh satisfies the same half-tube equilibrium as the exact field. If the matrix is integrated exactly, the same proof with integrals in place of sums gives \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = p_{\mathrm{a}}\,a\) for the stress from \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). The proof uses only that the constant \(1\) lies in the space of hat functions (step 2), just as for the truss, where the reactions balance the load because a rigid displacement lies in the space. The check therefore depends on the space and not on the quality of the mesh. We test it on three mistakes, each introduced into the computation of example 17.46.

  • A coarse mesh \(n = 1\). The sum is \(1{,}2\) MN/m \(= p\,a\) up to round-off, although the hoop stress at the bore is \(88{,}45\) MPa instead of \(78{,}00\), an error of \(+13{,}4\,\%\) (example 17.46). The check does not find the discretization error and cannot, because it holds on every mesh. It is found by comparison with the Lamé solution or by refining the mesh (check (f) of section 7.10.2, figure 17.29).
  • A wrong pressure in the data, \(p = 3\) MPa instead of \(30\) MPa. The sum is \(0{,}12\) MN/m, which is \(p\,a\) with the entered pressure, and it agrees with itself. If we compare it with \(p\,a\) at the pressure the task demands, the error is \(-90\,\%\). The check finds the mistake only when the computer has the true datum from the task, not from the input. Refining the mesh does not find this mistake, because the relative errors at \(p = 3\) MPa are the same as at \(30\) MPa (the computation is linear in \(p\)).
  • A wrong modulus, \(E = 19{,}6\) GPa instead of \(196\) GPa. The sum and all the stresses are unchanged (\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}(a) = 79{,}218\) MPa in both cases, because \(E\) does not enter the stresses of this force problem), but the displacement is \(168{,}71\ \mu\)m instead of \(16{,}87\ \mu\)m. Only comparing the displacement with an approximate or exact calculation (check (d)) or a review of units and data (check (g)) finds it. The stress check is blind to this mistake.

The list does not say that the real model is now verified. It says only which step catches which mistake. Section 7.10.2 did the same for the truss, and COOK lists mistakes that a program does not detect by itself: elements of the wrong type, a coarse mesh, supports wrong in position, kind or direction, a misplaced decimal point, and an element defined twice that we do not see on a plot of the mesh (COOK §10.13, PDF pp. 377-378). A program checks element distortion and unconnected nodes, but it cannot know whether the problem we wanted is the one defined, whether the material data are right, or whether the supports are in the right places (COOK §10.14, PDF p. 380). Since the program does not know this, the analyst must keep a record of the sources of data, assumptions, tests and the version of the program, so that after an interruption the work can be resumed or reviewed by someone else (COOK §10.13, PDF pp. 378-379).

17.9.4 Critique of the result and the decision

The sixth step is the critique. First the question whether the result looks strange, and then the quantities we already know (COOK §10.15, PDF pp. 380-381). COOK warns that stresses computed from displacements are less accurate than the displacements, so we do not trust them if the displacements are doubtful (COOK §10.15, PDF p. 382). In our tube the displacements are trustworthy but the stresses do not reach the boundary condition. At the bore \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -p = -30\) MPa must hold (theorem 11.27, step 7 of its proof), and the element at the bore gives \(-27{,}12\) MPa at \(n = 16\), which is \(9{,}59\,\%\) too little, and \(-28{,}54\) MPa at \(n = 32\), \(4{,}86\,\%\) too little. This deviation is an estimate of the error that needs no exact solution, because we know the condition from the task. The hoop stress is wrong by \(1{,}56\,\%\) and \(0{,}80\,\%\) at these two meshes, so the deviation of the boundary condition is six times larger than the error it estimates (\(6{,}15\) and \(6{,}11\)). The factor six is an observation on this tube, not a law: it says that the estimate is here on the safe side, and on another task it would have to be measured again.

If the critique finds a mistake, the dashed arrow sends the analysis back to the model and the mesh. The seventh step is the decision. The mesh with \(n = 16\) is within the \(2\,\%\) tolerance (\(1{,}43\,\%\)), but the error is one-sided and the deviation at the boundary says that the stress at the bore has not yet settled. So we use theorem 17.14. The order given by the two triples of meshes is close to \(1\) (\(0{,}93\) and \(0{,}96\)), so we take \(q = 1\), and from the values \(92{,}68\) and \(93{,}34\) MPa at \(n = 16\) and \(32\) we get \(2 \cdot 93{,}3449 - 92{,}6803 = 94{,}01\) MPa. The exact value is \(94{,}02\) MPa, an error of \(-0{,}013\,\%\), and \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 30 \cdot 220/94{,}01 = 70{,}21\) MPa. Had we taken the wrong \(q = 2\), which is right for the displacement, we would get \((4 \cdot 93{,}34 - 92{,}68)/3 = 93{,}57\) MPa, an error of \(-0{,}48\,\%\): within the tolerance, but more than thirty times larger than with the observed order (section 17.3).

The decision has a remainder that computing does not reduce. The discretization error at \(n = 16\) is \(1{,}43\,\%\), the difference between plane strain and closed ends is \(0{,}53\,\%\) and the difference between open and closed ends is \(3{,}2\,\%\). So we first decide what ends the tube really has (modelling error). Only then does it make sense to refine the mesh, since at \(1{,}43\,\%\) plane strain and closed ends (\(0{,}53\,\%\)) are not yet distinguished. For open ends \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 68{,}35\) MPa, the lowest of the three, and whoever does not know the ends designs by it.

17.9.5 Verification and validation

What the tables of example 17.46 do not cover is the question whether the model is the right one at all. ONATE1 has two terms for this and keeps them apart.

Definition 17.48 Verification and validation of a computational model (preverjanje in potrjevanje računskega modela)

Let a physical system be given, its mathematical model (equations and data) and a computational model (the solution of that model by finite elements). Verification is the process of determining that the computational model accurately represents the mathematical model and its solution, whether or not the model corresponds to reality. It has two parts:

  1. code verification: we gain confidence that the program solves the equations of the model correctly. It is done by comparison with simple cases that have an exact solution.
  2. calculation verification: for this computational case we estimate the discretization error, by refining the mesh or by raising the order of the elements.

Validation is the assessment whether the mathematical and the computational model represent the physical system for the intended purpose: by comparison with measurements on a model or on a real structure. A large deviation for an already verified program means that the chosen model is not suitable.

Source: ONATE1 §1.4.4 (PDF pp. 31-33): verification shows that we solve the problems accurately, validation that we solve the right problem.

The names say what they establish. To verify means in everyday use to look whether something holds, and verification here looks whether the solution holds for the model we wrote down. To validate means to establish by a measurement or a witness that something is so, and validation here compares the model with a measurement on the real system. For the tube, the first part, code verification, is the comparison of \(u(a)\) and the stresses with the Lamé solution (theorem 11.27): the exact solution of the mathematical model is the yardstick (the table in example 17.46, displacement \(0{,}004\,\%\) at \(n = 32\)). The second part, calculation verification, is the estimate from this section: from three meshes with Richardson's extrapolation and from the deviation of the boundary condition. For a tube with a groove, for which no exact solution exists, this would be the only part of verification we have for the computation itself, while the program would still be verified on the tube without the groove. ONATE1 also mentions manufactured solutions: we choose an arbitrary displacement field, compute from the equations the load that produces it, and check whether the program finds the field (ONATE1 §1.4.4, PDF pp. 33-35). Here we only name this way.

We have no validation for our tube. The book has no measured strains on a real tube, so the answer \(p_{\mathrm{Y}} = 70{,}2\) MPa (plane strain) holds for the model: a homogeneous isotropic linearly elastic material, the yield stress \(220\) MPa and the von Mises condition. It is verified and not validated. Among the unvalidated idealizations are these three: the material is homogeneous, yielding is described by the von Mises stress, and the ends of the tube are fixed as one of the three possibilities.

17.9.6 Software

The plan needs a tool, a program. Programs are not written by the average analyst but by researchers, students and companies, their development is expensive, and users stay loyal to the program they already know. For this reason COOK does not compare products, which change quickly, and neither do we name any. The documentation is part of the system we test, and it must be read when choosing a program (COOK, PDF p. 384). Code verification of definition 17.48 applies to a program we buy just as to one we write: the tube with the Lamé solution is a test that can be run on every program in which a pressure on the inner edge can be prescribed.

17.9.7 Plate with a hole: a plan without numbers

Chapter 11 left the question how large the stress at a hole in a finite plate is, and wrote it as the yardstick for a numerical result: Kirsch's factor \(3\) (theorem 11.51). The plate is \(200 \times 200\) mm with a hole of radius \(a = 10\) mm and a tensile load \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa, the largest stress is \(3\sigma_0 = 150\) MPa, first yielding is at \(\sigma_0 = 73{,}33\) MPa, and the error of the load at the edge due to the finite width is \(2{,}5\,\%\) (section 11.13.6). Let us see what the plan would demand for a finite element computation, and what we can already say from the book without a single mesh result.

Plane elements are in chapter 15, but the book does not carry out the computation of this plate with them, so there are no mesh numbers here. What we can compute is a yardstick for the mesh. Figure 17.30 shows how the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) along the \(y\) axis falls from the edge of the hole (equation (11.69)). First the axes: horizontally the distance from the centre of the hole in radii \(r/a\), vertically \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\sigma_0\). The curve starts at the peak at \(3\) and falls to \(1{,}93\) at \(r = 1{,}25\,a\), \(1{,}52\) at \(1{,}5\,a\), \(1{,}22\) at \(2\,a\) and \(1{,}07\) at \(3\,a\), towards the value \(1\) far from the hole. So the stress changes over a length of the size of the hole radius, and from here follows how fine the mesh must be.

An element in which the stress is constant cannot give the peak. The mean of a function over an interval is smaller than its largest value when the function is smaller than it everywhere except at one end, and the curve of the figure has its peak at \(r = a\). The orange segment shows an element of size \(h = a\) at the hole: the mean of the exact stress over it is \(1{,}6875\,\sigma_0\) (SymPy, outlines/ch-modeliranje/num-09.out), \(56\,\%\) of the peak. The blue segment at \(h = a/4\) gives \(2{,}376\,\sigma_0\), \(79\,\%\), and at \(h = a/8\) still only \(2{,}635\,\sigma_0\), \(88\,\%\). For small \(h\) the mean is about \(3\,\sigma_0 - 3{,}5\,\sigma_0\,h/a\): half the slope of the curve at the peak (\(-7\,\sigma_0/a\)), because the mean over an interval of length \(h\) is about the value at its middle. At \(h = a/8\) this approximation gives \(2{,}56\,\sigma_0\) instead of \(2{,}635\,\sigma_0\). The shortfall is therefore proportional to \(h/a\), and for \(2\,\%\) of the peak (\(0{,}06\,\sigma_0\)) a constant stress in the element would need \(h\) of about \(a/58\) (the exact mean gives \(a/57\), SymPy). This is why the plan for the plate uses higher-order elements or stress recovery (section 17.4), and refines the mesh towards the hole and not everywhere. The conclusion holds for elements with constant stress and does not say how much error the elements of chapter 15 would have.

The remaining steps of the plan follow the tube: a plane stress model of a quarter of the plate with mirror conditions on the axis planes (the idea of lemma 7.39, in general chapter 19), the question (the largest stress at a point at the hole, hence a mesh as fine as for stresses, section 17.9.2), the hand calculation (Kirsch's factor \(3\), the correction for the finite width is not computed, section 11.13.6), the check (the resultant of the forces on the edge \(x = \pm 100\) mm is \(\sigma_0 \cdot 200\ \text{mm} \cdot t\), like the reactions of the truss), the sequence of meshes and theorem 17.14, and the critique (the deviation of the value at the edge of the hole from the free-edge condition, as for the tube). Whoever gets a value near \(150\) MPa from the computation must not conclude that the mesh error is small: the difference from Kirsch's value also contains the effect of the finite width, which the book estimates only for the load on the edge (\(2{,}5\,\%\)), not for the stress at the hole. So we judge the mesh from three meshes and not from the comparison with \(3\sigma_0\).

17.9.8 What we have shown

The plan of an analysis is seven steps: question and tolerance, hand calculation, model, sequence of meshes, check, critique, decision (figure 17.28). On the tube we showed what each gives. The hand calculation hit the order of magnitude (\(60\) and \(75\) against \(78\) MPa), not \(2\,\%\) (with equation (17.44) and the Lamé field). The displacement and the stress converge at different speeds, \(0{,}017\,\%\) and \(1{,}43\,\%\) at \(n = 16\) (comparison of the columns of the table, figure 17.29). The check of the half-tube equilibrium holds on every mesh (lemma 17.47, proof with hat functions) and therefore does not find a coarse mesh, but it does find a wrong pressure if we compare it with the task (computed cases). The deviation of the boundary condition is six times larger than the error of the hoop stress (a computed case, not a law). Extrapolation with the observed order \(1\) gives \(94{,}01\) MPa against the exact \(94{,}02\) MPa. Larger than the error of \(1{,}43\,\%\) is the difference between open and closed ends, \(3{,}2\,\%\), and the mesh does not reduce it. The model is verified, not validated.

For the plate with a hole the plan is written without mesh numbers, because the book does not carry out the computation of this plate with the plane elements of chapter 15. The yardstick for the mesh, the mean of the exact stress over an element at the hole (\(56\,\%\) of the peak at \(h = a\)), is computed from Kirsch's solution.

17.10 Connections

The course abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19. Each section of this chapter treats one or two of the three errors that definition 17.2 in section 17.1 separates: the modelling error, the discretization error and the numerical error. For each section we say where its result returns, and for each connection also which error it reduces and which ones it leaves.

  • Hierarchy of models and the modelling error (section 17.1): lemma 17.3 says that the ratio of the shear part to the bending part of the tip deflection of a cantilever is \(E/(4kG)\,(H/L)^2\). For a steel cantilever with a rectangular section the Euler-Bernoulli model is below the Timoshenko model by \(16{,}32\) % at \(L/H = 2\) and by \(0{,}19\) % at \(L/H = 20\). The same question, when a one-dimensional model still suffices, returns for surface models in plates (MK, AK, chapter 18) and shells (MK, AK, chapter 22), and for flexible robot links, where the beam is the model of the link (DSK, chapter 28). No finer mesh reduces the modelling error: the Timoshenko model stays a beam model on every mesh (section 17.1).
  • Body to model, point force and submodel (section 17.2): theorem 17.9 proves that the total potential energy of a point force on a plane body is not bounded below, so by corollary 17.10 the displacement under the force grows without bound on nested meshes, while in a bar or a beam it does not (chapters 7 and 12). The load on a small area, which the point force replaces, is treated in chapter 25 (DSK). The submodel of lemma 17.5 rests on the uniqueness of the boundary value problem (theorem 11.4) and on Saint-Venant's principle of section 11.11. The half model of lemma 7.39 is extended by chapter 19 to mirror planes in several dimensions and to constraints between nodes (AK). The point force, the submodel and the half model are decisions about the modelling error, which a finer mesh does not correct.
  • Mesh convergence (section 17.3): the order of convergence from three nested meshes and Richardson's theorem 17.14 give for the first eigenvalue of a bar with both ends fixed, on three successive triples of meshes, the orders \(2{,}05\), \(2{,}02\) and \(2{,}01\) and an extrapolated value that differs from \(\pi^2\) by \(10^{-5}\). The same procedure holds for every quantity computed on a sequence of meshes, so also for temperatures (VT, AK, chapter 14) and for displacements of plane elements (AK, chapter 15). The discretization error falls as the mesh is refined, the modelling error and the numerical error stay.
  • Stresses from FE results (section 17.4): corollary 17.18 states the error estimate for finite elements promised by chapter 1 (the mean value theorem), and the stresses are one order worse than the displacements. The equivalent stress of definition 2.76 and the largest shear stress of theorem 2.70 are computed at the inner edge of the tube of chapter 11 from element stresses, which satisfy the boundary condition only in the limit. For continuum elements (AK, chapter 15) the Gauss points are the stress points, which is the same idea as the exact strain at one point of an element. A finer mesh reduces only the discretization error of the stresses, the modelling error and the numerical error stay.
  • Mesh quality (section 17.5): lemma 17.22 proves that the bar element with three nodes, its middle node at the fraction \(c\) of the length, has \(J > 0\) on the whole element exactly for \(1/4 < c < 3/4\). The letter \(J\) here is the one-dimensional \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}\xi\), in chapter 2 it is \(J = \det\mat F\), the ratio of volumes (lemma 2.55), and \(J_2\) is the second invariant of the deviator (equation (2.73)). For plane and solid elements the quality measures are only named, their Jacobian belongs to chapter 15 (AK). The quarter-point element (\(c = 1/4\)) captures a smooth field worse than the element with its middle node at the midpoint, and a field that behaves like \(\sqrt{x}\) exactly. The shape and the arrangement of elements change only the discretization error, they do not reduce the modelling error.
  • Large systems of equations (section 17.6): lemma 17.29 gives the condition number \(\kappa\) of definition 6.31 for a bar fixed at one end and free at the other, \(175{,}1\), \(16\,370\) and \(1\,622\,757\) for \(10\), \(100\) and \(1000\) elements. The band of the matrix from lemma 7.42 and one factorization for several load cases from lemma 7.47 remain valid for large models too. Constraints that chapter 19 eliminates from the system reduce the number of unknowns, while the penalty method keeps them and, by lemma 12.29, worsens \(\kappa\). The reduced model of chapter 21 shrinks the system to a few modes (DSK). The locking of continuum elements for a nearly incompressible material is a penalty system like the shear locking of the beam (AK, chapter 15). The section treats the numerical error: a finer mesh reduces the discretization error but raises \(\kappa\) and with it the upper bound of the numerical error.
  • Nonlinear statics (section 17.7): Newton's method, which converges quadratically when the tangent stiffness at the root is not zero, and theorem 17.35, by which a column made of a rigid bar with an imperfection and a horizontal spring has a limit load of \(0{,}931\) of the critical one at \(\theta_0 = 0{,}01\), complete the linear buckling analysis of definition 12.51 and the upper bound of theorem 12.53. The linear analysis gives the same critical load for both column models and cannot tell the stable model from the unstable one. Theorems 13.69 and 8.132 are about the perfect column, imperfections require a nonlinear model. The modelling error here is the linear model, which does not know the limit load, the numerical error is the stopped iteration, and a model with one degree of freedom has no discretization error. Plasticity and nonlinear contact are not treated in the book.
  • Nonlinear dynamics (section 17.8): the Newmark family of definition 17.36 contains the trapezoidal rule of chapter 10 (theorem 10.66) and central differences (theorem 10.70). Stability for one mode follows definition 10.65. For \(\gamma = 0{,}6\) and \(\beta = 0{,}3025\) the amplitude after one period at \(\omega\Delta t = 2\pi/20\) is \(0{,}9082\), which means that numerical damping damps the low modes too. Physical damping with a damping matrix (DSK, chapter 20) is a different notion and must not be confused with the damping of a scheme. For the pendulum of theorem 8.123, released from the horizontal position, the trapezoidal rule with the step \(2\pi/20\) (in units of \(\sqrt{l/g}\)) lengthens the period by \(0{,}57\) %, and unlike for a linear system it does not conserve the energy exactly (theorem 17.44). The step limit through the ratio \(h/c\) of chapter 13 holds for explicit steps. A smaller step reduces the discretization error in time, a more accurate Newton iteration the numerical error, and the modelling error (a point mass on a rigid rod, without friction and air) stays.
  • Plan of an analysis (section 17.9): the steps and checks of sections 7.10.1 and 7.10.2 and the split of errors of section 7.10.3 are the procedure, and section 17.9 applies it to the tube of theorem 11.27: the discretization error of the von Mises stress at the bore at 16 elements (\(1{,}43\) %) is larger than the difference between plane strain and closed ends (\(0{,}53\) %), while the difference between open and closed ends (\(3{,}2\) %) is a modelling error that the mesh does not reduce. Chapter 29 repeats the analysis in a loop, so there it matters which error each step reduces.
  • Planned in other chapters: plane and solid elements with the isoparametric map and the Jacobian matrix in chapter 15, symmetry and constraints in chapter 19, damping matrices in chapter 20, reduction and the eigenproblem of large systems in chapter 21, contact and Flamant's solution in chapter 25. Plasticity, large strains, the arc-length method, iterative solvers and mesh generation algorithms are only named.
  • Limits of the chapter: the error expansion \(e = C h^q + \dots\) for a general FE quantity, the number of lost digits of about \(\log_{10}\kappa\), the quality limits of plane and solid elements, the ZZ error estimate and adaptive meshing are cited from sources, not proved. Newmark stability is proved for a linear system mode by mode and only on the line \(\beta = (\gamma + \tfrac12)^2/4\), not for the general region \(2\beta \ge \gamma \ge \tfrac12\) and not for a nonlinear system.
